COMMON MEETING ROOM PROVIDED FOR MEMBERS AND THE GALLERY
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that representations, both last session and during the recess, were made to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) and to myself that there was a great need for a place in this building that would be a common meeting ground for members of the House and members of the press gallery. It was pointed out that with the present arrangement of lobbies and private rooms for members, there was little opportunity for intercourse between members. The minister and myself, after looking over the building for a suitable room, decided to place room No. 268 on the main floor, near the main entrance and opening out of the reading room, at the disposal of members of the House and the press gallery for the purpose referred to. The room has been furnished and is now open and ready for use.

INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT, 1907; AMENDMENT
Hon. JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
[Mr. Meighpn.l
On section 1-Statutory declaration to accompany application for appointment of Board.
Will the minister explain the purpose of the bill?

The change proposed in this section merely contemplates that, in cases where it has been impossible for employer and employee to meet and negotiate, a declaration may be accepted from the employees indicating that it has been impossible to secure a conference or enter into negotiations and that as a result a strike is likely to occur. There have been cases in the past where such a provision has appeared necessary.

There is before the law
courts on the way to the Privy Council for decision at the present time the question of the jurisdiction of parliament to enact legislation of this qature, and the question at issue is as to whether this parliament can delegate to itself the power to regulate the public utilities of municipalities. The municipalities operate many public utilities such as light and power, and under section 91 of the British North America Act it seems to me that this parliament has enough to do in reference to federal utilities, such as the postal service, without encroaching upon the realm of the provinces and the municipalities. I do not think that parliament should pass any legislation that has any relation to the municipalities without the consent of those municipalities. I understand that the Department of Justice has given an opinion that this whole act is ultra vires, and that opinion is supported by two courts of record in the province of Ontario. I think that is good not only as a matter of law but of policy. For how can this parliament say:	We are going to regulate the
municipal activities of, say, Winnipeg, Edmonton or Vancouver, and virtually act as a court of appeal in labour disputes between those municipalities and their employees? It is not in the public interest that there should be such interferences with the harmonious operation of public utilities by municipal corporations from the commercial aspect.
I should like to know who is asking for this legislation, because I understand the Department of Justice has advised that it is ultra vires of this parliament. Until the Privy Council has given its decision in the case now pending as to the respective powers of the federal parliament, the provincial legislatures

Industrial Disputes
and municipal corporations, I think it would be unwise to proceed with the bill. Certainly if it is enacted it will stir up trouble all over Canada, and the operation of public utilities by our municipalities will be very seriously handicapped. The present law is working quite satisfactorily, and our public ownership bodies are paying the highest wages to their employees. In my own province there is no complaint that the law is not working well. On all these grounds, therefore, I am strongly of opinion that we should leave well enough alone, or in any event defer action until we get the decision of the Privy Council on the case now in the courts which decision may be expected next May or June.

Mr. Chairman, I have been told that this clause is very favourable and very just to labour. But it is in one sentence a page long, and I can make neither head nor tail of it; I do not know what it means. I am reasonably certain that very few labour men would be able to interpret the clause. Therefore I would ask the Minister of Labour to kindly explain once more what it really means, because I did not get his first explanation.	*

If my hon. friend from
East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) will look at the explanatory notes on the right hand pages he will find that the only changes proposed are printed in italics, their purpose being to permit the acceptance of a request from employees for a board of conciliation, even although those employees are not able to declare that they have met the employer and exhausted negotiations. As long as they can declare that they have made all possible efforts to obtain a satisfactory settlement, that will be sufficient for the Department of Labour to act upon.
Might I say to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) that the particular question which he dealt with is not referred to in any of these proposed amendments? He is quite correct in saying that a board appointed by the Department of Labour was enjoined from proceeding with an investigation in regard to certain employees of the Hydro-Electric Commission in Toronto. An application was made to the department, and .following the usual practice of many years the department asked the Hydro-Electric Commission if they would agree to the formation of a board. The Commission hesitated for some time and finally did, in substance, decline to give their sanction to the formation of such a board. The department regarded the situation as so important that it proceeded to appoint a board, and the Hydro-Electric Commission at once took proceedings in the courts to obtain an injunction, which injunction the department has scrupulously observed. But we went into court to ascertain the rights of the federal Labour department under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. One judge issued the injunction and another judge, of equal standing, disagreed with his learned brother and referred the case to the Court of Appeal of Ontario, where argument was heard about a month ago. A decision is expected in a few days. As my hon. friend from North Toronto suggested, the case will probably go to the Privy Council for final determination. I may say that should it be decided that we have no right to appoint a conciliation board in the case of disputes between municipal corporations and their employees, it would simplify our work very much. But the proposed amendments have no connection with the question raised by my hon. friend, and I am quite sure he will not contend for a moment that the act is not applicable to recognized dominion-wide public utilities. The particular section we are now considering has no bearing on the case before the Court of Appeal.

Will the hon. minister
go a step further and tell the House what the result would be, if the proposed amendments are passed, in the case of a strike of the employees of any government department, and the department in question refused to negotiate with the strikers? Could the strikers thereupon go to the minister's department and as a matter of right obtain a board of conciliation?
I could not say what I might do or the department might do until we were confronted with the circumstances and were able to take them into consideration.
Similar cases have arisen in the past, so it is nothing new. We had a similar case in Winnipeg, where a department refused to treat with strikers.
I never before heard it intimated that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act applied to such disputes.

As I understand the act, and as the hon. gentleman has endeavoured to explain it, it would seem to apply to any body of organized labour.
Industrial Disputes
The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act applies to public utilities which are specified in section 2 of the act. The Post Office Department would not be a public utility as contemplated by the act.
Will the minister read section 2?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is an amendment to section 15 of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. It is a question whether that inquiry is in order.

The whole question of the power of this legislature to enact a law of this kind is now before the courts, and if the act is declared unconstitutional then this amendment would also be unconstitutional. If the act applies to municipal public utilities, why should employees of the Post Office Department not be given a board if they wish to make a declaration under the act? Moreover, they are getting only one-half what the Hydro-Electric employees are getting to-day. Their lowest wage is $790 a year whereas in the other case it is $1,200 or $1,300. I contend that this whole matter should be held over until next session pending the decision whether this parliament has power to pass legislation of this kind.

What is the meaning of
the exception in parenthesis in lines 13, 14 and 15, section 1 (b), which reads:
Except where the application is made by an employer in consequence of an intended change in wages or hours proposed by the said employer.

That parenthesis has been there for a number of years. It does not contemplate any intention of an employer to lock out his employees, but he may have a justifiable intent of serving notice on his employees of his desire for a reduction of wages, and in that case he could make the necessary declaration.
Does the minister look upon the post office as a public utility?
Not within the meaning of this act.

Does it cease
to be a public utility because it is looked after by a department of the government?

Not so long ago it was
even held that this act did not apply to Intercolonial Railway employees because they were government employees. I think several decisions to that effect were made.

That is what I
want to get at: The real distinction is that they are government employees, and that is why the department does not consider that the act applies.

One other important
reason is that they ax-e not engaged as employees of a public utility as specified in section 2 of the act.

Why on earth
the whole act was placed in jeopardy through an endeavour to make other public officials, just as representative of the people as this body, subject to what we would not make applicable to our own people, I do not know. It is idle to say that there should be regulation of public utilities simply because they happen to be provincial in their character while on the other hand the same regulation should not apply to public utilities which are carried on by the Dominion government.

The other evening while
we were discussing the resolution of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) I made some observations with regard to the necessity of having changes made in our constitution, the British North America Act, which would clearly define the respective powers of this parliament and the provincial legislatures with regard to labour and several other matters. The opinions of judges of our supreme courts, especially in Nova Scotia, with which I am more familiar, are such that there is grave doubt in the public mind whether parliament had the power under the British North America Act to pass this legislation. In a private discussion which I had with the minister the other day he suggested to me that there would shortly be a decision which would settle the question. I presume that he had reference to the case to which the hon. member for North Toronto has just referred. In that case the question may not be brought fairly before us whether or not the act is ultra vires. The case may turn on the question of whether it is a provincial public utility or a national public utility. I for one would like to see

Industrial Disputes
the Privy Council decide just as clearly and as quickly as it can be done whether the Industrial Disputes Act is within the power and-jurisdiction of this parliament. I am one of those who think that the Industrial Disputes Act has been a tremendous power for good in this country. Innumerable disputes which would otherwise have led to strikes and disasters have been averted through the goodwill which was brought about between employers and employees by virtue of this act, and so far as I am concerned I would be sorry if in the end it was declared ultra vires by the Privy Council. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) suggests that the Department of Justice has given opinions which, in effect, declare the act to be ultra vires.

Merely against
the municipality.

As against the municipality. I read some of these opinions last winter, and I am sorry to say that different branches of the Department of Justice have given different opinions as to the validity of this act. I hope the day will soon come when if this case is not taken direct to the Privy Council-and if the Department or Labour loses the case in Toronto they certainly will carry it to the Privy Council, but in case the Department of Labour wins, the people of Ontario may not see fit to carry the case to that court-
They will.

Then that will overcome the difficulty. I have my own opinions as a lawyer, very serious and, I think very well-grounded opinions. I am not going to give them to the House this afternoon; I did give them more or less the other day; but I think this matter should be settled. There should not be any doubt about the matter, and if there should remain any doubt after the decision of the Privy Council, if they do not give a clear-cut decision as to the validity of the act, I think the Department of Justice should even take the trouble of having our constitution so amended as to make it perfectly and amply and fully plain that this parliament has the power to legislate on matters of this kind.
I do not think the Industrial Disputes Act goes far enough. It seems to me that in all our great industries in this country there should be the means whereby a conciliation board could be granted, in order to give employer and employee a chance to fight their differences out before such a board. Let me give an instance. In the constituency I
represent we have two great industries, the coal mining industry and the steel industry.
If differences of opinion arise in the coal mining industry, and if the conditions of the act are fulfilled, the employers may get a board, and boards h|ive done very much good in that part of the country; but if a difference of opinion arises between the steel workers and their employers, who are the very same people, the British Empire Steel Company, the poor steel worker is told that he cannot have a board to investigate his grievances, while his brother, the fcoal miner, working for the same corporation five miles away, has the right to a conciliation board.
I would draw this respectfully to the attention of the Minister of Labour. It may make for a weakness in the act so far as legislative power is concerned, but I think the day should come when this parliament should take power under the constitution to give every industry, employers and employees, the right to a conciliation board. Let not a preference, so to speak, be given to a man because he happens to be working in an industry which comes under the nomen of a "public utility."

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Relation of parties to remain unchanged pending proceedings before a board.

There is one point, it semes to me, that is hardly sufficiently guarded in this clause. The idea is that there shall be no change pending an investigation. If I am rightly informed in the case of the Nova Scotia trouble a year and a half ago, a board had been asked for, but the employers took the ground that since the agreement had expired there could be no change in the conditions; that is, they had been running along under the conditions of the old agreement, but the agreement having expired the employers took the ground that everything was at an end, and they proposed under those circumstances to change the rates of pay, the hours and working conditions. It was really that that led to the so-called "ca' canny" policy-"striking on the job," the men taking the ground that since there was no agreement they were not bound to give a certain amount of work. Now it is quite obvious that the company was not carrying out the spirit behind this legislation, and I wonder whether it would not be possible to draft the legislation in such a way that no employer or employee could disregard its spirit in that way.



Industrial Disputes
Even although the agreement had come to a close at the end of the year, could not the conditions run along until a. final settlement was made? I would ask the Minister of Labour if it would not be possible to insert such a clause as that?

1 fear it would be impossible to attempt to meet the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth), for this reason: It would contemplate coercion possibly of both parties to an agreement, and we might have just as much or even more difficulty in securing the consent of the workmen than of the employers to a provision of that kind, which would, in effect, tie them to their tasks for a certain stated or uncertain time. I am sure we would have just as much difficulty under the circumstances suggested by my hon. friend, where you would compel the workmen to continue working under the conditions of an agreement after it had expired until a board had finished its sittings and had filed its award.
Do you not do that m this case?

We hope to secure the co-operation of both employer and employee to the end that no interruption of the industry's operations shall take place; but we would hope also to secure the co-operation of the employer and employee in seeing that agreements be not made that would automatically sever relations as between the two parties at a given time. The consistent thing,
I think, for organized labour to do now generally is to make an agreement subject to sixty days' notice of a desire for a change by either party to the agreement. That would give reasonable latitude to the interests of the parties and the public for negotiations to be held and a new agreement to be reached.	.
Now, in the case my hon. friend cited the agreement expired at a certain hour on a certain given day, and, no new agreement having been arrived at, there was a complete stoppage of operations regardless of the public right in the matter, creating a situation which ought to have been avoided. But I suggest to my hon. friend that such a situation cannot be avoided by attempting to assert in this, or in any other law, a coercive restriction that will compel either the employer or the workman to continue operations, possibly in the case of the latter, at a rate he may not have agreed to.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: - The only object of the bill is to correct two words in the French version. The word "earliest" in the fourth line of the English version-you have it on the opposite page-was translated into French as if it were the "latest". The translator who would translate "black" into "white", and "earliest" into "latest" needs an examination. Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to amend section six of the Northern pacific Halibut Fishery Protection Act, chapter sixty-one of the statutes of 1923, which relates to Canadian and United States nationals and ships liable to seizure for engaging in fishing for halibut in prohibited waters, by limiting the time for an offence thereunder to the close season as defined in the Act, and by repealing section nine, relating to the seizure of foreign ships.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The committee will surely remember that, following the treaty between Canada and the United States, an act was passed during the last session in order to make' effective the provisions of the treaty. The first amendment which is proposed relates to section 6 which reads:
Every national or inhabitant of Canada or of the United States, and every ship, vessel or boat registered in Canada or the United States, or belonging to a national or inhabitant of Canada or of the United States, together with all furniture, apparel, appliances, gear, tackle and rigging thereof, engaged in or used in connection with fishing for halibut in prohibited waters or aiding or facilitating, or used for the purpose of aiding or facilitating such fishing, may be seized by any officer authorized by the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act to board and search.
41i
The amendment is to add the words "during the close season" after the words "prohibited waters." As the section now stands, it prohibits fishing throughout the year, the words "during the close season" having been left out through error. We propose to repeal the whole section because, by a rule passed last session, when we amend part of a section, we have to repeal the whole section and ask that a new one be substituted for it.
The next amendment we have in view is to repeal section 9 which reads:
Every ship, vessel or boat which is foreign, or not navigated according to the laws of the United Kingdom or of Canada, which,
.	(a) has been found fiishing or preparing to fish or to
have been fishing for halibut in the territorial waters of the western coast of Canada in any close season; or (b) has entered such waters for any purpose of which the execution is prohibited by this act: may be seized by any of the officers aforesaid.
Section 9 is almost a repetition of section 5. The point covered by this section is already covered by section 5 which reads:
Every ship, vessel or boat, including all furniture, apparei, appliances, gear, tackle and rigging thereof, which is in any manner operated or used for the purpose of committing an offence against this act, or for aiding or facilitating the commisson of any such offence, may be seized by any officer authorized by the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act to board and search, and shall be forfeited;
Besides that, section 9 may be objected to on account of the fact that it states that only foreign ships can be seized. It appears that an exception is made in regard to vessels navigating according to the laws of the United Kingdom or Canada. I think these small . amendments will not in any way change the situation in which we find ourselves now. They are not material at all. They are intended only to do away with some doubts which may arise between the interpretation of section 9 and section 5.

I should like to suggest to the minister that, in making the amendment, he might, perhaps, go a little further in section 6. The act itself defines the territorial waters of the western coast of Canada. It also defines the territorial waters of the United States. I cannot conceive that a Canadian customs officer would be intended, by this government, to attempt any seizure outside of our own territorial waters. Yet, if my hon. friend will look at section 6 as it stands to-day, he will find that apparently just as much power is given to a Canadian customs officer to seize at Seattle as there was for him to seize during the open season. I quite concur that it is correct to limit this legislation
Pacific Halibut Fishery

to the close season; but I think it would be just as well to make it clear to men who are looking to the statute for guidance, that their operations as regards seizures ought to be confined to the territorial waters of Canada. I would suggest for the purpose, not of criticism but of assistance, that after the word "seized" in the printed statute at the third line from the top of the page, there should be some definition of the place, that is, seized "within the territorial waters of Canada" or some similar expression, because I can understand how a zealous but mistaken officer might cause considerably difficulty by going outside of Canadian territorial limits altogether and making a seizure.
I would also like to suggest that section 9, which the minister proposes to repeal, might receive further consideration. Section 4 puts the owner or master of a vessel under a certain penalty. Section 5, as the minister very properly says, involves forfeiture of any vessel:
-which is in any manner operated or used for the purpose of committing an offence against this act, or for aiding or facilitating the commisson of any such offence.
I think that might very properly apply to vessels on our own register. I would think, however, that we would not be wise, to say the least, to attempt to create an offence or to inflict a punishment upon a foreign vessel, unless her act had been done within the ports or territorial waters of Canada. Under section 4 or section 5, it does not matter where the person or the vessel is. For instance, if a Canadian vessel were out on the high seas and made preparations there to invade the territorial waters of Canada for the purpose of illegal fishing, I think this law would apply and we could punish our own nationals.

Has my hon. friend read the treaty under which this resolution is framed? It will be found. I think, that there was entered into between Canada and the United States an agreement which gives to Canada, under the treaty, authority to seize United States' vessels which are found in Canadian or American water if they are violating the provisions of the treaty, and the Americans are to have the same powers regarding Canadian vessels found in Canadian or American waters. If Canada seizes United States vessels, she must hand them over to the United States for trial, and the same thing would apply in regard to Canadian vessels seized by the United States, the United States would have to hand them over to 
Canada for trial. If power were given to seize vessels only in territorial waters, you would not get them at all, because it is only in extra-territorial waters that the offence is committed.

Perhaps in a spirit of great national charity I was not designating the people of the United States as foreigners. As regards foreign ships, I was thinking of ships other than those of the United States. I had in mind the provisions of the treaty as my hon. friend has them in mind, although Pm blessed if I know whether there is a treaty or not. Perhaps my hon friend knows.
, Mr. MARTELL: There will be.
Oh, there is to be.
It is in esse. It only needs ratification.

I have no objection to a treaty. The only thing is that this treaty appeared as a New Year's gift in some of the newspapers, and it has appeared several times since with little strings, tails, fins and little wiggly things all around it. A few days ago it came into this House as a subject of ratification. It did not matter if we were riding chariots through the Civil Service; it did not matter if we had forgotten how to cut down rates; it did not matter if we had stagnation in the Maritime provinces, a subject in which the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) ought to be interested-the great constitutional thing, the great light that had developed on the world, the great beneficence m the twentieth century was that a Canadian could sign his name upon a piece of parchment and bind some part of the British Empire; that is, if the thing was unilateral, or bilateral, or quadrilateral, or based upon some other angles that were not defined. My hon. friend wants to take great comfort out of this signature. I will tell him that I very much prefer to get down to something that has real meat in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is fish.

It is all very well to indulge in flights of imagination, but really nobody cares a bit whether we sign treaties on this side of the Atlantic or on the other side; what we do care about is that we shall get something out of them. That is the real point.

When we were last in committee we had under consideration the estimate for completion of the tower and there was a suggestion that the government should explain to the House what delay in this work would mean not only in the actual cost but also from the point of view of the deterioration of the tower itself and of the buildings that have been used in its construction. I indicated at that time that the architect's commission was fixed at 5i per cent for completion and that we had an arrangement with him to complete the construction. The plans have been prepared and are being submitted to the department under that arrangement. If we should decide to
cancel our arrangement with the architect he would be entitled to receive from us 3 per cent on the plans to date, and at the end of five or six or ten years, whenever we might decide to complete the construction, we should either require to make a new contract with the present architects or engage another architect. In that case our expenditure would involve an additional 7 per cent in all probability, following the usual architectural fees, because we could not have the benefit which we should otherwise have in having the present architect complete the work. The first item of 3 per cent on the completed tower, on an expenditure of $565,000, would be $16,950; and the commission which it would be necessary to pay if we started to work over again, would amount, at 7 per cent, to $39,550. In regard to the contractor's commission, our arrangement is that he should complete the work at the old commission of 7 per cent. I believe that those who have had experience with contractors and who are familiar with work of this character will realize that the completion of, this tower is probably one of the most difficult portions of the construction of the parliament buildings, and I have no doubt that if it became necessary some years later to enter into a new contract the builder would expect a larger percentage than even 7 per cent. Indeed, the officers of the department are of the opinion that it would cost at least 10 per cent; and on an expenditure of $480,000 that additional 3 per cent would mean an addition of $14,400. Now, if we should decide to delay construction for five or six years,
I think it must be evident to all who know anything about	the	surroundings	of	thesebuildings that it would be necessary to clear the debris from the grounds and do other work of that kind, and we should have to have the grounds sodded and put into proper shape. The estimated cost for the removal of buildings used in construction, and of stone, brick, sand and other material, in addition to the cleaning up of the ground and	completing	the work	of	paving	grading	and	so forth,	is	$20,000.We have a very large workshop on Sussex street which was erected primarily for carving and cutting the stone to be used in this	building.	It	is built of	substantial
timbers and equipped with cranes and other machinery necessary for the handling of heavy stone. When built in 1916 it was not expected that it would be required for more than four or five years, and I am informed that last year it was discovered that dry rot had attacked the foundation timbers, neces-

sitating the insertion of concrete blocks to maintain the structure in place. If we should decide not to proceed with the programme now contemplated, it will be necessary to tear down the workshop and from the timber construct a shed of sufficient size to store the stone and other material that will eventually go into the tower. That is estimated to cost $82,000. This figure includes the cost of removing the machinery and either installing it in a new building or else taking the stone to Montreal or some other place to be cut and carved, which means heavy cartage and freight charges. It will be seen therefore that any delay will entail a very considerable expense, in fact it is estimated by the department that about $172,000 will be the price of delay. It was suggested a few nights ago in discussion that so many hundred thousands of dollars at five per cent interest would mean so much money, and by delaying construction there would be a saving of this interest. But as a matter of fact instead of being a saving there would be a very considerable loss. Besides this, hon. members will no doubt have noticed that the sandstone used in this building darkens on exposure to the weather, and if we should delay construction for a period of years, there will be a marked difference between the new and the old work. In the course of years the two would probably blend harmoniously, but for some years after completion we would have the upper third of the tower sticking up like a sore-thumb.
Now, I think it would be unwise for the committee to entertain delaying this construction. It is part of the scheme undertaken years ago after the fire, and I hope hon. members will be of the opinion, after the information I have just given, that we would be ill advised to delay the work. I might say that when the estimates for my department were first submitted to me by the officials they asked for a vote of $800,000. We have since reduced this total by $200,000. It was a rather difficult proposition to undertake, and it was not easy to arrive at conclusions that would be satisfactory both to the architect and contractors and to the people of this country, but a settlement was made that I think upon examination will be found to be very satisfactory. We shall spend only what is necessary. Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (.Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
He said:	The bill before the House is
identical with the measure which was introduced at the last session, with the exception that an alteration has necessarily been made in the year. That bill, as hon. members will recall, passed its second reading, and was referred to a select committee of the House which reported at the end of the session as follows:
The special committee, to whom was referred the Bill No. 15, an act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, beg leave to present the following as their third report:
Redistribution

Your committee held several meetings since its appointment on the 22nd of February last. The preparation of the schedules to be annexed to the said Bill was entrusted to sub-committees. The greater number of such sub-committees accomplished considerable work and have, from time to time, reported progress to your committee. It has been found, however, that differences of opinion exist, and your committee have decided that it would be unable to complete the schedules before prorogation.
They therefore have agreed to report back the Bill without amendment, and recommend that a similar committee be appointed at an early period at the next session of parliament to consider such Bill.
Your committee also recommend that the letters, maps secured from the Department of the Interior and papers produced in the course of its proceedings remain in the possession of the clerk of the committee until the next session of parliament, and that the same be produced by him at the first regular meeting of the newly-appointed committee.
Your committee also submit herewith a copy of the printed proceedings and evidence taken before them for the information of the House.
This report is to be found in the votes and proceedings of June 29, 1923. On the motion of Dr. Beland (for Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) the third report of the special committee to whom was referred Bill No. 15 to readjust the representation in the House of Commons was concurred in on June 30.
I need scarcely remind the House that the government, in bringing forward this measure, is not exercising any discretionary power, but is simply discharging the duty which is imposed upon it by the constitution. The law, as hon. members know, provides that after each decennial census there shall be a redistribution of the seats of this House, and since confederation there have been several redistributions some complete and others in part.
When introducing the bill last session I dwelt upon this matter at some length, and it is hardly necessary to go over the entire ground again, but as some of the questions that are likely to come up in this debate may perhaps be best answered by anticipating them, I may repeat to the House a few of the essential facts that bear on the question of redistribution.
First then, as to the redistributions which have already taken place: There have been since confederation several redistributions. The first Was made in 1872, the next in 1882, the next in 1892, the next in 1903; the last redistribution was made in 1914. There have been partial redistributions for the purpose of providing for the representation of provinces which were not in the Dominion when confederation was originally formed. There was a partial redistribution in 1871 to give Manitoba representation; a partial redistribution in 1887 to provide for the representation of the Northwest Territory; and there [Mr. Mackenzie King.)
was a partial redistribution in 1907 to provide for the representation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta which were subsequently formed out of the Northwest Territory.
In 1915 an amendment was passed to the British North America Act relating more particularly to the province of Prince Edward Island. It was in the nature of a partial redistribution, and added to the British North America Act as section 51a the following provision :
Notwithstanding anything in this act a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of Senators representing such province.
By section 1, subsection 1 paragraph 2 of the Act to Amend the British North America Act, 1867, being 56 George V, Chapter 45, the representation of Prince Edward Island in the Senate was fixed at four members. The census prior to that partial redistribution would have affected the representation of Prince Edward Island to the extent of the loss of one member, but for this amendment which provided that no province shall have in the House a smaller representation than it has in the Senate.
Another partial redistribution was made to give the Yukon territory representation in the House of Commons. The Yukon territory obtained its right to representation under the act known as the Yukon Territory Representation Act, 1902, assented to on the 15th May, of that year. The clause that relates to this matter reads:
The Yukon territory as that territory is defined and constituted by section 13 of the schedule to chapter 41 of the statutes of 1901, shall be an electoral di3tiict. and shall return one member to the House of Commons of Canada.
The Yukon territory received its representation under the redistribution of 1903.
Perhaps it would be well also to put on record for the convenience of members the sections of the British North America Act which bear specifically on this matter of redistribution. The pertinent sections are as follows:
Section 37. The House of Commons shall, subject to the provisions of this act, consist of one hundred and eighty-one members, of whom eighty-two shall be elected for Ontario, sixty-five for Quebec, nineteen for Nova Scotia, and fifteen for New Brunswick.
Section 51. On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such a manner, and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules.
(1)	Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five members:	.

Redistribution
(2)	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained) :
(3)	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded; but a fractional part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number:
(4)	On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at
the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards:
(5)	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
Section 52. The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.

Let me now say a word as to the method which the government proposes to adopt in effecting this redistribution. In the old days, the government of the day brought into the House a bill in which the several constituencies were already delimited or defined. The government itself prepared the redistribution map, if I may so name it. As hon. members who have followed the political history of the country know, this method was looked upon as more or less arbitrary, if not indeed very arbitrary, and as giving to the government of the day, in virtue of its powers, opportunity for shaping constituencies pretty much as it wished, and thereby effecting what was commonly known as a gerrymander of the constituencies. In 1903, a different principle was introduced. Sir Wilfrid Laurier when in opposition had always contended that this was not a fair method of arranging the redistribution of the House of Commons. He contended that this arrangement should be made the subject of conference between the different parties in the House, and that both the government and the opposition should choose from their membership, a certain number to serve on a select committee, to which committee the bill dealing with this subject of redistribution would be referred. In the bill the number of members to which each province was entitled was set forth; but the actual defining of the several constituencies was left to the select committee with instructions to report back to the House after they had made out the redistribution map. That practice, which was adopted in 1903 for the first time, seemed to work so well that it was again followed in a 
subsequent redistribution after the census of 1911. That would be the redistribution of 1913 when Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister of this country. We propose, as we did last session, to adopt that method this year, and to have chosen from both sides of the House a limited number of members as a special select committee to whom will be referred the bill in the form in which it has been presented to the House, with a space for the actual constituencies in blank to be filled in by the committee. We will ask the committee to fill out the schedule and to report to the House its negotiations in this particular.
In this connection, I think it ds well that we should make clear the lines on which we would expect the committee to proceed. There are guiding principles wihich have been observed in the past and which, experience would seem to indicate, it is advisable should be strictly adhered to. The first of these is the principle of following county municipal organization as a basis in whatever may be done in arranging the constituencies. There are obvious reasons why this should be a guiding principle. The municipal organization is the basis of our entire judicial system, of our municipal system, and by holding to the county unit, municipal organization, we are following a basis that is familiar to citizens of the country generally. It might be of interest to the House for me to quote briefly a word or two from former political leaders in this House as to the particular motive which they have had in advocating that this principle be followed. It was first asserted by the Right Hon. Sir John A Macdonald in 1872, at the time of the redistribution of that year. I have copied from Hansard of June 1 of that year-page 928-the remarks of Sir John A. Macdonald at the time, and they are almost as applicable at the moment as they were in 1872:

It is desired, as	much	as	possible,	to keep therepresentation within the country so that each county that is a municipality of Ontario should be represented, and if it becomes large enough, that it should be divided	into	ridings-that	principle is
carried out in the suggestions I am about to make.
It is obvious that	there	is	a great	advantage inhaving counties elect men whom they know. Our municipal system gives an admirable opportunity to constituencies to select men for their deserts. We all know the process which happily goes on in western Canada. A young man in a county commences his public life by being elected, by the neighbours who know him, to the	township	council.	If he shows
himself possessed of administrative ability he is made reeve or deputy reeve of the county. He becomes a member of the county council, and as his experience increases and his character and abilities become known, he is selected by his people as their representative in parliament. It is, I think, a grand system that the people of Canada should have the opportunity of choosing for political promotion the men in whom they have most confidence and of whose abilities they are fully assured. All that great advantage is lost by cutting off a portion of two several counties and adding them together for electoral purposes only. Those portions so cut off have no common interest; they do not meet together, and they have no common feeling except that once in five years they go to the polls in their own township to vote for a man who may be known in one section and not in another. This tends towards the introduction and development of the American system of caucuses, by which wirepullers take adventurers for their political ability only, and not from any personal respect for them. So that, as much as possible, from any point of view, it is advisable that counties should refuse men whom they do not know, and when the representation is increased it should be by sub-dividing the counties into ridings.
That, Mr. Speaker, is, I think, good, sound doctrine. Unfortunately, although it was enunciated by Sir John Macdonald, his government, I am afraid, did not always act in accordance with it. They departed so much from the principle that it became necessary later	to get back to	the principle
originally intended, and in 1899 a bill was introduced in this House by Sir Wilfrid Laurier for a partial redistribution, or in other words a redistribution to undo the wrongs that had been perpetrated on the electors of Canada in 1882 and in 1892. In bringing in that measure Sir Wilfrid Laurier enunciated the same principle, in the following words:
I may say at once that the object we have in view in presenting this bill is not to make a total redistribution of the electoral districts under which the House of Commons is now constituted. We deem that it would not be -expedient at this time to do more than undo, so far as we can, the most glaring violations of a principle which we have always held, and which has always been universally held by public opinion in this country, to be the fundamental principle of representation. We think it is a principle which will commend itself universally to public opinion, that the basis of representation in this House should be the municipal county organization. It is in the recollection of all the members of this House that this principle was to a large extent interfered with
by the Redistribution Act of 1882. That act was a violation of the principle which had prevailed up to that time, and had been maintained not alone by the Liberal party, but by the Conservative party as well. There are many well-known reasons why the municipal county organization should be preserved as the basis of representation.
It is upon that basis we shall expect the committee to whom the present bill will be referred to proceed.
There is another principle which has been followed in previous redistributions, recognized by all governments from the time of confederation down to the present, and that is that, as respects the unit of representation, the unit for the urban constituencies should be larger than the unit for rural constituencies. The reason of that must, I think, be apparent; indeed, there are several reasons, the most obvious of which I shall mention. In the first place, the people in rural areas are scattered over a very much larger area. It is not possible in a widely scattered community to organize public opinion as readily as it can be organized in more thickly settled parts. Moreover, in the urban centres there are recognized organizations ready to hand, for the purpose of focussing public opinion at any particular moment. For example, there are the boards of trade that exist in the cities, and such institutions as the modern clubs and associations of business men which we have to-day. Again, the press of the cities is a much more potent, or, at 'least, is a more constant, factor than the press of the rural communities; it has a power of influencing public opinion and of keeping the urban, point of view continuously before the people-of the country. Further, it is I think a recognized fact that many rural constituencies are represented in parliament by members who reside in urban centres and who have a knowledge of urban conditions, perhaps in some cases even more intimate than they have of rural conditions. The reverse of that is not, I think, equally true; it is not often that a city is represented, at least in this parliament, by a member who resides for the greater part of his time in the country. These are all reasons which in the past have caused committees which have had to do with the work of redistribution to recognize the justice of permitting a larger unit for the urban constituencies than for the rural. I confess that the introduction of parties representing a class, if they are rightly to be so regarded, would be to my mind a reason for departing from that principle; but I hope that parliament will not become representative of classes as distinct from representatives of the people as a whole. It is important, I
Redistribution

think, that all classes should be represented; but class representation would be in my opinion opposed to the point of view *that-a candidate when elected to parliament represents all the people from the community from which he comes, irrespective altogether of the classes to which they belong.
And that brings me to the third consideration which should be a guiding principle in the shaping of the electoral districts, that, namely, of the compactness of districts. An effort should be made, within county boundaries or within recognized defining lines as between urban and rural centres, to have constituencies as compact as possible so that public opinion within one given area will be as nearly true to the feeling of the whole community as it is possible to get it.
I think the one remaining important principle is that of maintaining, both in the case of representation in rural areas and in the case of urban areas, an equalization of population as between constituencies. The reason of that is obvious. It is desirable that the different constituencies should be, so far as may be possible, very much on an equality in regard to the numbers of the persons who compose them.
It will not, be possible of course, for the committee to work out a redistribution, following county municipal organization along the lines which I have indicated, with mathematical exactness. That has never been found possible, and never will be; but in this as in all matters common sense and fair play should be our guide. That is really the purpose of having a bill of this character referred to a committee, and it is also a reason why such a committee should not be too large in size. The idea is that a few members, well inten-tioned, may sit down around a table and work out a scheme to be presented to the House. It is not the intention to take away from the Commons their right to pass upon whatever may be the outcome of the committee's deliberations. The intention is to relieve this House as far as possible of a cumbersome load, of a duty which, with such a large membership, it could not begin satisfactorily to discharge. We want to get a few hon. members together around a table, actuated, as I s&y>
by principles of fair play and justice to all, and have them work out a schedule of constituencies, and then to present it to the House for endorsation, amendment or rejection. It is with this end in view that I shall later on if the second reading carries, as I expect it will, move the appointment of a committee to whom the bill will be referred.
The government has but one object in view,-that the committee, following broadly [Mr. Mackenzie King.}
the principles which I have indicated, shall work out on the basis of the new unit of representation the electoral districts for the representation of this House on lines which will commend themselves to the sense of fair play and justice of hon. members and of the people generally, so that this House of Commons may be, as far as possible, a true mirror of the public opinion of our country.

It is not very many years ago-in my lifetime, Mr. Speaker-when it was necessary to have property in order to vote; for a long time the chief qualification for voting was the ownership of property. And if we go a little further back we shall find an exceedingly restricted franchise based upon the ownership of property. Well, we have been getting away from that, and the ownership of property does not now exercise so much influence as it did in earlier days when we had a much more limited franchise which led to very many and grave abuses.
My right hon. friend gives us some reasons why there should be a higher unit of representation in the cities than in the rural districts. One is that, in the latter, population is scattered and is not easily organized. That argument might have been good enough twenty-five or thirty years ago, but it is not
of any weight to-day. T1 f rural districts of every province enjoy goi d roads and the people there own motor oars; the press is scattered daily by the rural mailmen to every home in the farming districts; and I presume that by the time we have another general election radio will be added to these means of communication. So the farmer will be able to sit in the comfort of his home before the grate fire and listen to the speeches of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and some of the other spellbinders of the Liberal party as well as of those of this party.
"The Prime Minister suggested that the cities could be organized more easily than the rural districts. I doubt that very much. What with farmers' clubs and the widespread distribution of daily papers, the rural districts can be organized about as quickly as the cities. We have had proof of that: The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) knows it very well. He could go out and organize a rural riding in the course of a month or less, and get it working intensively, unitedly, and, as we have evidence on this side of the House, effectively. The argument that the population is scattered, therefore, entirely loses weight. As to some rural ridings being represented by men who live in the cities, why, that is a matter of choice for the electors themselves. No man can go out from a city and steal a seat from a man living in a rural district, against the wish of the electors. If the electors prefer to have a lawyer represent them rather than a farmer, that is a matter for themselves; so I do not think that argument can be used in favour of a difference in the unit of representation.
My right hon. friend refers to the class organizations that we have now. Well, they are before our eyes. How long that will last * is a matter of conjecture. It did not last very long in Ontario; it may last longer in the western provinces. But whether it lasts or not, the fact that those interesed in the agricultural industry are so organized, places them, I submit, upon a parity with those who are organized in industrial life, and they should not ask, and should not receive, any greater favours in the way of added influence than the people who live in the city. Why should a mechanic have less political influence than a farm labourer? Why should his vote count for less? He is just as intelligent a unit of this population; he works just as hard and contributes just as much to the welfare of the country. Why does it take two men living in the city to have the same influence as one farmer? Well, the unit of population is 36,283 as applied to the rural

districts, and if I understand the scheme properly, the unit for the cities is about 67,000. Why, we will have rural districts with a population of probably 26,000 or less. Upon every ground of justice to men and to women I submit that there should be the same unit in the cities as there is in the rural districts.

Toronto ought to have fifteen seats and Montreal nineteen or twenty. We should look upon people as human beings, we should not deal (Mr. Hocken.]
with the matter simply from the point of view of the length of time they have lived on a certain piece of land. People are born m the cities; they live in the cities all their lives, and in my judgment they do not move about in any greater proportion than do the people in the farming districts. We have heard a great deal from our friends to the left about the exodus from western Canada. Well, if the population is maintaining its size, there must be as many coming in as are going out, so that the population in the agricultural districts in the West is changing just as it is in the big cities. I believe that that change takes place to as large an extent as it does in any of the urban centres.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this point should be taken into consideration by the committee. The government ought to lay it down as a policy that there should be an even unit of population for the cities and the rural districts; otherwise you increase the influence of one class of the community, \\hich, I submit, is not fair. I have no thought in my mind that any man living in the agricultural districts should be discriminated against, and I would not for one moment suggest that his influence should be minimized or lessened as compared with that of people m other parts of the country. But I do not think it is fair to those who live in cities and who contribute as much as they can to the welfare and progress of this country- as much, I think, as any other class of people that there should be this difference in the unit of representation. From the results of their labour come the great bulk of the taxes that pour into the national treasury, and if their work can produce the revenues necessary to keep this country going I do not see why they should be discriminated against when it comes to their casting their ballots m a general election.
I know that there are so many more members here representing rural constituencies than there are representing urban constituencies that my argument is not likely to prevail with them. But if they are fair, if they have a mind to be just and to deal fairly with Canadians in all parts of this country they will give the cities the same representation in proportion to population that they ask for themselves. That is all I have to say, Mr Speaker; I simply wanted to present these views before the bill went to the committee in order that, before it was too late, they might be presented for consideration.

The hon. member also referred to the fact that the country districts had been able to organize themselves. The only explanation I can offer for that is the justice of their cause and the absolute need for organization to protect their interests having regard to the interests of the better organized city centres. They are not organized in any spirit of antagonism to the cities. It seems to be taken for granted by some hon. gentlemen in this House that when we speak for the rural districts we are speaking in antagonism to the cities. I want to repudiate any such idea. I have no antagonism against Toronto or any other city;

Let me speak of the constituency of which I know most, and it is a fair type of the constituencies of western Canada. During the last election some of my constituents had to drive fifteen miles to the poll. That meant a drive of thirty miles to and from the poll. In my constituency, to vote means a drive of thirty miles for some- of my constituents. That alone, I think, is quite sufficient, without any further argument to show that the unit of population in the urban districts should be larger and in the rural districts smaller.
I was pleased to hear my leader say what he did about class representation. I have tried since I have been here, and I think every other member has done so-and succeeded remarkably well-to take a national point of view in matters that come before us.

I feel compelled to offer a word,
perhaps a suggestion. I am sure the Prime Minister, in common with everyone else in the House, realizes that Canada is top heavy with governmental machinery. I wonder, however, if the Prime Minister has ever thought what an opportune time this would be to reduce the representation in the House. As a result of that reduction I should perhaps be one of the first to fall by the wayside, but the constituency of Portage k Prairie would still remain. I should therefore like to suggest that the number of members be reduced by approximately one-third. It is true that the population of Quebec is really the pivotal point of our representation but in the course of events it is altogether possible-some may say it is not probable-that the other provinces will outstrip Quebec in the matter of population.

It is not, to my mind, a question of bringing the unit to an exact level, but I do say an effort ought to be made, if possible, to make the margin of difference a little narrower than it has developed into during the last twenty years, under the last two revisions. Quite a lecture was read to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) because he put up a rather strong case. Naturally he was arguing from one particular viewpoint, and I think he put up a very strong case. It is in my estimation desirable that large cities like Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Hamilton, and such like, should have fair representation. I am quite prepared to admit that, as regards my province it would be unreasonable to expect an exact division or representation by population. For instance, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride), who I see is in his seat, represents a riding, which, I think, is at least one thousand miles in length. He has in his riding alone, a territory larger than some of the provinces-larger than several of the provinces. It would be absurd to ask that the unit of representation there should be brought up to the level of that in the cities. The same thing, to a lesser degree, applies to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Mae-Kelvie) and perhaps to the members for East Kootenay (Mr. King) and West Kootenay (Mr. Humphrey). We have in British Columbia at least four or five ridings that would extend from 400 to 1,000 miles in length. Those are very extended territories and very difficult to get over. So, it would be absurd I think, to ask that the unit of representation should be the same throughout the province. On the other hand, we shall have, as I say, in the riding which I will represent at least seventy thousand, even under the amended law.

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext: I brought that out in the remarks which I made on this question last year, and I feel quite flattered that eminent journalists like Mr. Gratton O'Leary have been [DOT]publishing certain figures which I gave last year.

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend is flattered, but I want to put this viewpoint before the House,-Mr. O'Leary seems not to have published this-that no cabinet minister in the United States ever has to appear in congress; the cabinet ministers of Canada spend half their time in the House during a session of parliament. If you allow the members of the Canadian government to remain in their offices for twelve months in the year, not to have to appear on the floor of the House, not to have to prepare speeches, not to have to be responsible to the people, you can cut the number of .cabinet ministers in Canada in two quite easily and they will not have to work half as hard then as they have to work now. There is another point. The number of cabinet ministers in Canada has been compared with the number in Great Britain. The practice in Great Britain is altogether different from the practice in Canada. In Great Britain you will seldom see, except on special occasions, more than one cabinet minister in the House, and that will be when something under his particular charge is being discussed. The cabinet minister in Great Britain is represented in the House by an under-secretary who takes charge of all details of legislation. Furthermore, if you desire to interview a cabinet minister in Great Britain you are bound to make an appointment with him a long way ahead, whereas the cabinet ministers of' the Canadian government -and rightly so-are only too glad to meet members of parliament at any time, day or night, while the House is in session.
What I am trying to point out is that the comparison is not a fair one as regards the number of cabinet ministers in Canada, because the duties of the cabinet ministers in this country are far more arduous, so far as legislation is concerned, than those of the ministers of the Crown in Great Britain; while from the standpoint of general work those duties are far greater than the duties of members of the cabinet in the United States, comparing the sessions of our parliament with the sessions of congress.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont):
maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
The question of representation in this parliament is one of great importance and interest to the Canadian people, and of course it is well that the matter should be settled along certain definite lines and in accordance with certain definite principles. I agree with the principle that as far as possible county boundaries should be maintained, for the reasons as given already by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I might refer also to the fourth principle, that of maintaining as far as possible, as between rural constituencies, a uniformity of population. Where there is a conflict between these two principles, the principle of maintaining county boundaries and that of maintaining uniformity in population, the question arises as to which of them should be sacrificed, and whether or not it is to the advantage of the people as well as of the members that county boundaries should be maintained even though there may be a great disparity in population. The question often arises, if county boundaries are to be maintained, where a large town or a small-sized city happens to be in one county and a neighbouring county happens to be practically all a rural population. I am rather of the opinion that the people are more concerned in maintaining their county boundaries than they are in having population nearly equal as between county constituencies. So that in my opinion the fourth principle should be sacrificed to the first when there is a conflict between the two.
I am interested in the discussion that has arisen on the second principle, namely, that the unit for urban representation should be larger than the unit for rural representation. That has always been recognized; it has been recognized by all governments and all parties in this country ever since confederation. In the last redistribution, that of ten years ago, under the government of Sir Robert Borden, the unit of representation in the city of Toronto was 50,000, when the unit for the whole Dominion was in the neighbourhood of some 30,000.	*

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext: It is getting worse.

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
That was a disparity that was recognized at that time as a proper difference as between rural and urban population. If today the unit of representation is to be 36,000 for the whole country, the unit of representation for the city of Toronto in the same proportion would be about 60,000 which would not entitle that city to more than nine
