members. There is another question that enters into a consideration of this matter, as referred to by my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Hammell), and that is the interest which the people in a constituency take in public affairs. I remember that not long ago the question was debated in this country whether or not electors should be disfranchised when they neglected to use their franchise. If that is to be taken into consideration at all it will be instructive to see what interest the people of Toronto have shown in public affairs. I have just jotted down the number of voters who voted for candidates in the last general election. I do not know what the population of Centre Toronto is but I believe it is considerable, and of the large number of electors there only 11,161 took enough interest in the election to cast their vote. I represent a rather small rural constituency and in that riding 16,224 persons voted in the election. In another constituency in Toronto, East Toronto, just 15,002 electors voted at the general election in 1921. I do not know how many voters were on the list because I have not the figures with me; I just jotted down these facts a few moments ago. In North Toronto the people showed some more interest in the election, this being due perhaps to the popularity of one of the candidates running in that constituency. At any rate, 20,985 persons voted in that constituency. But the very popular representative from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard), and all the candidates running in that constituency, could not induce more than 7,566 electors to vote; while in West Toronto 11,764 persons voted. And in the beautiful city of Brantford, represented by my genial friend across the way (Mr. Raymond), 13,049 electors voted in that election. These figures I think give us an indication of the interest which the people in these constituencies tal e in public questions. I have taken at random a few rural constituencies. I do not know whether they are large or small as compared with other rural constituencies, but they will illustrate my pointy I have already given the constituency of Glengarry and Stormont. In the constituency of Carleton 13,473 electors voted; in Dundas, another small rural constituency, 11,225 voted; in Durham, 12,516; in North Grey, 14.996 and in Halton, a small constituency, 12,207 persons cast their votes. So that in all these rural constituencies, as compared with an equal number of urban constituencies which I have picked at random, the vote in the country was larger than the vote in the urban centres, with the exception of North Toronto; and although the dispar-

ity in population may be very great the disparity in representation is not so great after all. That is, I think, an added reason why in the coming redistribution the unit of representation for the rural constituencies should be very much smaller than that for the urban constituencies.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, personally, I do not want to enter into any very detailed consideration of our * cities or towns, but I should like to express my general accord with practically everything that has fallen from the last speaker (Mr. Kennedy). I hesitate, in discussing this subject, to touch upon any province other than my own. I believe if there is one matter more than another which we should endeavour to keep our hands off it is the very delicate question of representation, and that so far as it is possible to do it each province should rather settle that for itself. I do not mean through the agency of the local legislatures, of course, but through their representatives in this House. The problem of Toronto or of Montreal is a purely local one having relation to the population and representation of the rest of Ontario or Quebec. The conditions there cannot be thoroughly understood by a man in the Maritime provinces, and it would be presumptuous for me to discuss representation in British Columbia or in the three western provinces. The people there know the local conditions far better.
The conditions in my own province, of which I will Just say a word, are these:	A
comparatively stable population, changing not very much even in the cities, though changing there more than in the rural districts, with the cities of course constituting compact constituencies. All you- have to do is to ask any candidate whether he would rather run for a city or a rural constituency, and the answer unhesitatingly will be that he will run for the city constituency, because it saves him a tremendous amount of work and is much easier to keep in touch with. Therefore, so far as my province is concerned, I would favour, to whatever extent may be necessary, a larger unit for the constituencies that include cities, and a smaller unit for the purely rural districts.
But I would not stop quite there. I admit that if you apply pure theory to this matter, one man is just as good as another, and should have just as much to say as another, and in order to give him an equal opportunity, you ought to make everything mathematically equal. But you cannot do that in human affairs. That is the practical answer; and

Redistribution
in our form of government sentiment, to my mind, plays a far greater part than mathematics. There are one or two instances in my own province, small though it may be, where the people have grown around a certain centre and have their well-defined boundaries. There is, for example, the shire town towards which all eyes look; it is the political home of both parties. If, except under the greatest necessity in the world, you disrupt that and try to force those people into new relations with other parts of the province, you are going to cause far more dissatisfaction than you will confer benefit. You do not, at present, perhaps, have mathematical equality, but you do have a rough and ready measure of justice for the people who are accustomed to certain conditions, which conditions it is not worth while to disturb. Therefore in a province like my own, where there is no change in the total number of representation', I would say:	Let
conditions remain as they are. They have been fair enough in the past. My province has never had to protest against anything in the nature of a geriymander, and there is no reason for unduly disturbing conditions. Those are the principles that, so far as they may be applicable, I should like to see applied throughout Canada-simply a spirit of fair play and no more unncessary disturbance than you are obliged to make to fit new conditions.
Nor would I draw too strong an inference from the number of people who have voted at one particular election. Another element enters there,-the very human element. It is partly the issue, and it is also partly the candidate. Now, I do not think you can build up a very strong argument because in the city of Toronto a large number of people did not think it worth while to turn out to secure what was no doubt regarded as an inevitable result in that city. But when you get into other constituencies, whether rural or urban, in any of the provinces, you will find that just in proportion as you make the contest a doubtful one you will bring out a much larger voting strength; and a very great deal depends also upon the personalities of the candidates. Those are factors which are not always equal. Perhaps even deductions drawn from a number of elections would not have much value. All this can be dealt with, not under a basis of representation, but by a consideration of the suggestions put forward as to whether it is not time to treat the franchise as no longer a privilege but an absolute and imminent duty, and to regard a man as failing in the duties of citizenship who does not exercise his franchise. Even if he does not
care for any of the candidates, it is at least his duty to make a choice of the least objectionable of two or more evils-a duty which ought to be discharged by every voter.
But for the present all I would say is: Let us approach this matter of representation in a broad, fair, non-political spirit, not with the idea of jockeying for party advantage, but to give the people the fairest and best opportunity of getting representation if they can, and realizing that those candidates who have to travel hundreds of miles in order to seek the franchises of the electors, or those electors who have to travel scores of miles to record their votes, are entitled to some more consideration than those who have only to spend ten or fifteen minutes for the purpose.

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext:
A good deal has been said as to the
disadvantages of rural residents, and. as to . the necessity of giving them a larger representation, Might I point out that these disadvantages are not quite so real as has been suggested? In a good many countries there are several towns and occasionally small cities, but the greater number of the people are rural. That sometimes gives the rural people a decided advantage, because some candidate can be proposed who is very largely acceptable to them, and on the other hand there is no one living in the little town who is sufficiently strong to carry the whole majority of the people throughout the riding. It seems to me that there can be no real basis other than that of representation by population. But I would agree with the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) when he suggests that in certain peculiar constituencies where the geographical situation is such as to make the population very scattered there may need to be certain modifications. But certainly the idea ought to be as near as we can approximate to it that one Canadian's vote is just as good as another's, and should be as fully represented on the floor of this House.
There is another point, moreover, that I should like to mention. The Prime Minister said that as far as possible it seemed wise to maintain the county as the unit. We in the West do not know a great deal about counties, but I suggest that if this principle is to be applied to well recognized units such as eastern counties, it ought decidedly to be applied in the case of cities. That has not been the case in the past. I think now of one of our western districts where three constituencies centre into one city. In each the representative is a rural member, and that quite large city has been effectively deprived of any representation in this House.

It would seem as if, to carry out this principle of fairness* the city ought as far as possible to be regarded as a unit.

Surely the reason for that lack of interest is the lack of anything like proportional representation. When people are confident that one side only stands a chance of winning, they can hardly be induced to go to the polls. If there were grouped constituencies where the minorities would have some chance of electing a man to represent their special viewpoint, a great deal more interest would be taken in the election and the various cities would be represented on the floor of this House much more nearly in accordance with the real opinion of their people. Whether or not the system of proportional representation is generally adopted at this time, I would urge that it be given a fair trial in one or two cities. In the city of Winnipeg we have for some years been accustomed to proportional representation in municipal and provincial affairs, and I think I am correct in stating that the large majority of the people of that city are well satisfied with the proportional representation system. We are accustomed to it; we have found that it works well, and we can see no reason why it should not be tried out in federal affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the well defined principles enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the guidance of the committee are eminently fair, but it seems to me that some other principles that are also vital may have been overlooked and possibly will not be considered by the committee. One of these is that existing boundaries should be regarded as closely as possible, and another is that cognizance should be taken of the railway facilities. There are particular cases already, I understand, where it has been suggested to cut a small country town completely off from a large part of the country that it serves. I have one particular case in mind of a plan drawn up where the country on one side of this town is cut off right at the boundary of the town. I think that is not altogether fair. With regard to adhering to existing boundaries, I think that is very, very important. Take, for instance, a constituency that has about sixteen municipalities. I have one in mind at the present moment. We will say that there are four municipalities east and west, and four north and south, sixteen in all. Under the new plan it will still have sixteen municipalities, but two rows are taken off the north and added on the west, which would mean that the new constituency is half the width it was before and double the length. Now it is impossible to have that constituency properly served in such a case, and it seems to me that these two factors should be taken into consideration by the committee.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

I beg to move:
That Bill No. 2 intituled "An Act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons" be referred to a special committee, the names of the members of which to be given at a later date, with instructions to prepare schedules to contain and describe the several electoral divisions entitled to return members to this House, and to report the same.
I am sorry not to be able to give the names of the committee to-night, but I would point out that on two previous occasions a motion was presented in this form.

maintopic: GENERAL AND PARTIAL REDISTRIBUTION OF FEDERAL CONSTITUENCIES
speechtext: Of course, the motion as it is drafted would not be accepted in the British House of Commons, because no question can be referred to a committee unless the committee is appointed and the members of the committee named. But as the right hon. the Prime Minister states we have two Canadian precedents. I have one just now which is fresh in my mind. On the 3rd of May, 1921, the right hon. the Prime Minister of the day referred Bill No. 2, "An act to amend and consolidate the law relating to Copyright" to a special committee to be subsequently named, after it had been given its second reading. The motion passed and the next day, the 4th of May, the special committee to consider the bill was appointed, consisting of several members. I presume the right hon. gentleman intends to follow that precedent, and under those circumstances I would consider that with the unanimous consent of the House the motion is in order, although it would not be in order in the Mother of Parliaments.

Perhaps my hon. friend would allow me to complete what I have to say about the building, and I shall be glad to answer questions later.
For at least twenty-five years the government of Canada has been trying to secure in London suitable accommodation for the offices of the High Commissioner and such other officials as this country has in the capital of the Old World. Lord Strathcona, while High Commissioner, endeavoured unsuccessfully to obtain a suitable building, as also did Sir George Perley when he was overseas in a similar capacity. Since he has been High Commissioner, the Honourable Mr. Larkin has been endeavouring to find adequate and creditable accommodation, and although at first he also was unsuccessful he has been extremely fortunate in being able to acquire a building occupying one of the finest positions in the world. The building is situated on the corner of Trafalgar Square and Cock-spur Street; and notwithstanding an incredulous smile which I observe opposite, I repeat that it is the finest site that could be obtained in the world.

The finest

I repeat, it is something of which we may be proud that Canada has been fortunate enough to secure what may well be regarded as the finest site in London, and, being in London, the finest in the world, for its offices in England. In regard to the necessity for these offices, it is all a matter of how one wishes to view the status of the Dominion. Australia has exceptionally fine buildings in London; South Africa a couple of years ago acquired on the other side of Trafalgar Square a building known as Morley's hotel which it owns to-day. Canada, on the other hand, has been in an obscure position notwithstanding that she is the leading dominion; and, so far as she has been known to the people in London by any distinctive building, she does not appear to have been on the map, so to speak, until the change of position of which I have been speaking. I might mention that there are also in London at the present time offices of the provinces of Canada. The province of Nova Scotia has finer offices for its agent than has the Dominion for its High Commissioner; and British Columbia has a building which is infinitely superior to ours. Indeed, when we sought last year to purchase their building from the government of British Columbia for the Dominion of Canada we could not acquire it. A stranger visiting London to-day and knowing little about Canadian affairs might think, from the accommodation enjoyed by the respective governments, that Canada was a part of British Columbia instead of British Columbia being a province of the Dominion. When we tried to acquire from that province the building which it owns in London we discovered that the provincial government had found it so good an investment, notwithstanding that it was a very large building, that the province refused to sell it. _
A feature that should be taken into consideration in connection with the present purchase is the importance of the site, which of course is a most important element in the selection of a building.' And there is the further fact that this particular building happens to be on ground which is the property of the Crown in Great Britain, and that may prove an all important consideration should it come to a question of renewing the lease at some future time. So far as the Dominion government is concerned, I hope it may expect to receive from the British gov-

ernment at all times fair treatment in the matter of the lease which it will hold, and the opportunity to acquire a property such as the one that we have secured might never come again. It was a mere chance that the Union Club was prepared at that-moment to give up the site and move to another part of the city. Had it been generally known that the site was available it is extremely doubtful whether the Dominion government W'ould have been able to acquire it; but the matter having been ' negotiated quietly it was possible for us to secure this highly desirable accommodation.
Although it does not bear directly upon the matter under consideration, I might mention at this time that we have no official residence for the Canadian High Commissioner in London. It is my opinion that the country ought to own its own residence in London for its representative. It did originally own a residence, at the time, I think, that Sir Charles Tupper was High Commissioner. That residence was subsequently disposed of when Lord Strathcona provided one on his own account. However Mr. Larkin, the present High Commissioner, has purchased a very valuable residence in London and is u-ing it in the service of the country in a very generous way. He happens to be well-to-do and is prepared thus to use his money in the service of the country. I think Canada is under a great-obligation to him by reason of his willingness to further her interests in this way apart altogether from the important duties he discharges m connection with his office as High Commissioner. This building is conveniently situated in relation to important railway, banking, commercial and business institutions, and it can be reached from any part of London by underground railway. In short, a better site could not possibly be obtained. I might add-a matter that came to my attention while I was in England- that the building which South Africa purchased only a few years ago had a lease of ten years to run; the Corporation of the City of London have decided to widen the space at the entrance to the Strand and have arranged for the expropriation of the necessary ground, which means that the Morley's hotel building is to be torn down, and the width of the Strand as it approaches Trafalgar Square will be considerably greater, than it now is. I mention that because it is a factor, once this alteration is made, it will vastly enhance the value of the building which we have secured. Mr. Chairman, last year I was rather favourable to the provision of Canadian offices in London. My idea was that we would, in a measure, emulate Australia in gathering together all our offices in one building. When you go down the Strand you see a large white building which is known as Australia House, and it contains all the offices of the states of the commonwealth. When you look for a Canadian House, you have to go down the Strand where you find a small building'that you might pass a dozen times before you would know that it contains the offices of the provinces of Ontario Then you go up by Trafalgar Square and down another little street to find a splendid building representing British Columbia. flhe attraction is not so much architectural as the ex-

hibition made by British Columbia and the interest which their agent is taking in his work. Then you go by Westminster and eventually reach Victoria street, and there you nd in an out-of-the-way place the offices of our High Commissioner. Last year my idea was that we were to get together with the provinces and gather all the offices, both federal and provincial, under one roof and have a truly Canadian House, similar to Australia House. Now we are asked to vote a large sum of money. For what? To remove the offices of the High Commissioner only from away down at 16 Victoria street up to Trafalgar Square,-to a site where the traffic is very small. We are simply expending this large amount of money for the removal of the offices of the' High Commissioner from Victoria Street to 1 rafalgar square, and we are making no effort whatever to co-operate with the provinces in the matter. This is an expenditure which I do not feel like supporting, and I do not intend to support it. I have not been in consultation with anybody else, but I do think it is a scheme that Canada will not be very proud of. The offices of the soldiers-a very small affair, I think-will be removed from somewhere about Oxford street, but these offices will gradually go out of existence. It seems to me that Canada should co-operate with her provinces with a view to federal and provincial officers being located in a building that Canadians can be proud of. If a Canadian from Ontario goes over he finds his own little provincial house on the Strand and then he will find the Dominion house up on the far side of Trafalgar Square. I say it is not a condition that we should be proud of, and I do not think any person who has been in London will be proud of it either.

I am most pleased to hear the remarks that have been made to-night about the British Columbia building. When that building was erected the provincial government was ridiculed from one end of the province to the other. It was alleged that there had been graft in connection with the transaction and that the property would be a white elephant on the hands of the province. But here to-night it is held up as a sort of example of good business and as something that Canada has reason to be proud of. I am more than pleased to hear what has been said and I have no doubt that if this building is purchased for the purposes that have been mentioned it may have the same history.

representative of British Columbia had something to do with the business ability that has characterized the activities of British Columbia m London. That building now-and I would like hon. gentlemen to be sure to hear this- is carrying itself.

At present the High Commissioner has some rooms in a building on a corner of the Haymarket. I drove down there to hunt up the High Commissioner and I discovered that I had to find him out among a lot of other people who were occupying the building. He is the only representative of an overseas dominion whom it is difficult to find in London. Canada loses immensely by having her High Commissioner housed in a building which is altogether unfitted for
a representative of this great country. I went into this building on Trafalgar Square. It has a splendid location. I do not know whether you could build another storey on it or not, but I do know that it looks out on Trafalgar Square and that the daily traffic past this building is such that more people will be brought in touch with Canada in a few months than would be the case in ten years on Victoria street. Surely it is not a bad investment for Canada to have a building of her own in the heart of London if we intend to continue to do business in the metropolis of the world. Australia has her representatives disposing of her products in London, and I think the same applies to New Zealand. We have not gone that far, but perhaps we shall want to go that far before very long. Our first step, however, is to provide a building worthy of this great Dominion and to let the people of London and the people of the world who go there know, through our High Commissioner, through our Trade and Commerce department and through our Immigration department, just what we have in this country. I have enough faith in Canada to believe that when the people of the world know what Canada is and what we have, we shall have no trouble in filling up our vacant spaces in this great country. British Columbia has made money on her investment, and I have no doubt in the world but that Canada could in a few years sell her equity in this property for much more than she is paying for it to-day. I do not look upon an investment where you are getting value for your money as throwing ^way your money at all. It is not an expenditure in the ordinary sense of the word; it is simply transferring cash into its equivalent in real estate, and the real estate in this case will bring to the people of Canada, to my mind a return in every way. Our citizens when they go to the great metropolis will not be ashamed to say, "I am from Canada", for Canada has now a suitable place for her representative. If it were a private concern acting under the same circumstances I think they would consider it a good investment, both nationally and commercially.

Mr. Chairman, I am one of those who would like to see a Canadian building in London. I have always harboured that hope, and I do not want it to be represented that the reason it was not acquired under the late government was that we could not find one. That was not the reason according to my recollection. The reason was that we had so much other expenditure to take care of that we thought it would have to wait. The hope at that

time was-and I did not know it had been abandoned, apparently it has only been abandoned during the last few months-that we would be in the fulness of time, when we could afford it, get a building in which the representatives of all the provinces could be held. I know that British Columbia now has a building in London and a fine one. I suppose they made a good real estate investment. I do not want to withhold credit from them, but really I do not feel like falling down in adoration before the financial or commercial discretion of a government merely because real estate has gone up in value. Nor do I share the argument of the minister that this is going to be a paying thing because real estate in London is going to go up more in value. I do not know whether it will or not; I do not think anybody else knows whether it will. A great many people have often thought real estate would go up, and now are very sorry that they thought so, and the experience of Canada may be the experience of England. No one knows. In my judgment-not that I think it is worth anything, I do not think the judgment of anyone here is worth anything on this matter-but for myself, knowing present real estate values in London compared with what they were before the war, I would rather be on the bear end of the market if it were the right and proper duty of the government of Canada to be speculating in real estate.
But, coming to the right course to pursue to-day, it is not to buy with the idea that real estate is to go up; that is not our function at all. Our functidh is to get, at the proper time, a site for the purpose worthy of our country. Now, I would not want to give up hope that Canada could have a building in which the provinces yet would come,-and possibly British Columbia, which has a little debt, might be disposed to apply its profits upon its real estate in London to that debt. They may not be so disposed. They have a perfect right to decide themselves what they are going to do with it. But I do not like the idea of the provinces of Canada being separately represented over there in separate buildings scattered all over the city of London, to appear in adverse fashion before various departments. I would like to see them all together, and I would like to see a whole lot more cohesion in the representation of this Dominion in the capital of the Empire. Surely it is not too big a thing to look for that Canada will have a unit representation there, not nine-representatives there, not ten representatives there, some working not in consonance with but in competition with the others-striving for the highest seats in the

synagogue and all the rest of it. It is not a spectacle that is alluring and it does not seem to me consonant with the structure of confederation that this individual representation should continue, and especially in isolated fashion in the Motherland.
Now, even according to the minister's hopes, based on the unspecified predictions of the Commissioner over there that he is going to be able'to house four different departments in this building, though upon the best information we have here- 11 p.m. for the minister has none at all-
_ it is only the size of that now occupied by his own department, one of the four, and is going to cost us $36,000 a year more than the other four together. Besides, notwithstanding the encomiums passed upon the building by the Prime Minister, I learn from other information maybe not as good, and I may as well mention one of my informants and only one, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black), who is pretty well acquainted with London, that this building is on a street close to a heavily travelled street but not itself heavily travelled. It is near to being a good site but it is not the best by any means. But would it not be better to wait and try to work out what we have been struggling towards, and also wait till we are in a better financial position than we are in this year of grace? Do not let the minister imaging that he is going to get this in shape by spending $300,000 on it. It is not going to be in a very alluring condition when the British Empire Exhibition is on. I hope we will have a display at that Exhibition which will be a credit to Canada, without our having to buy a $1,250,000 or $1,500,000 building in order to have a side attraction.
It seems to me the part of wisdom to get along as we are for the present. We managed in other times and right up until the war was well on, to entice a- large volume of immigration here, even though we had no very pretentious office in London, and I fancy that it we have good wholesome conditions in Canada we will get immigration here. The volume of our immigration is not going to be enlarged by the size of the window panes of a building in the middle of London, but by the letters home of the people who get work in Canada. That will affect immigration much more rapidly than the character of the building we happen to have in any section of the capital. That is my suggestion to the government. I do not yield to anyone in the pride I feel in the fact that some day we will have a home there worthy of the whole Dominion, and not merely one that

It so happens that this building adjoins the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons, and had the government felt that parliament would be prepared at this time to purchase the entire frontage facing Trafalgar Square, and which would give to the Canadian building an entrance on Cockspur street and also on Pall Mall East, I think the government might have proceeded with an effort to secure the building of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons as well.
I am told it cannot be secured.

That 'is one reason, I think, why we .ought to take this site while there is a chance to take it. More than that. We could not renew it unless we were prepared to take it for another term of years. The government did not feel it would be justified in leasing such a building for another five or six years; it was long out of date many years ago, and at the present time we have come into temporary quarters. We are there only for the period of a year with the right of renewal for another year; there is no certainty we will be able to stay there any longer. All these circumstances have to do with the
considerations which, in the government a mind, make it imperative to purchase the site at once.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me a finer site in the world than Trafalgar Square?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I certainly will. There would be a beautiful site for this building where the British Columbia building is on Waterloo Place. But, talking of Trafalgar Square, this building will be on the dead side. There will certainly not be so many people passing on that side of Trafalgar Square or Cockspur street as pass 17 and 19 Victoria street where the offices of the country were before.
Nonsense!

My hon. friend says
"nonsense". He has certainly not had experience or he would not make that remark. At this time when the country is being asked to save money where it can this purchase should not be made. How was it Lord Strathcona could live and carry on business on Victoria street, also Sir George Perley? But we have a new High Commissioner now and the idea is that money should be spent and spent in large amounts. I am against this vote, and I think that everyone who knows the location and the facts will be of the same opinion. In conclusion, I pin my judgment to the letter of Messrs. Knight, Frank & Rutley whom the government got to support this purchase.

I am once more amazed to find the great interest taken by hon. members to our left in expenditures. We have two expressions from that quarter on this vote; one from the leader of the party in his usual critical terms, to the effect that it is unfortunate that this vote came this year. Well, if it is unfortunate that the government proposes to spend this money this year, surely it is unfortunate that the party to our left sit quiet, without protest, prepared to allow the vote to go through.

Do you not want a
chance to speak?

No, I was not looking for
a chance to speak. All I was looking for was a chance to vote against this item, and I am going to see that I get it. Like my leader (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross), I do not think any member is more anxious to see the government properly housed in London or more anxious to see justice done to Canada in Great Britain than I am. Canada has done very well as the leading British dominion for a great number of years, with immigration that largely exceeds the immigration of today from Great Britain, with immigration that largely exceeds the immigration that we can look for from Great Britain for a period of years to come, and I think we can reasonably say that that business was fairly well handled by our former High Commissioner. As I stated the other day, w'hat we are here for, particularly this year, is to see that every item of capital expenditure that is proposed by the government and that we can do without this year or for a period of years to come, should be cut out ruthlessly from the estimates. What is the effect of passing these various items of capital expenditure that we can do without? It means that the promise contained in the Speech from the Throne for a reduction of taxation cannot be carried out, unless that reduction in taxation is the mythical reduction in taxation on agricultural implements by reducing the tariff. That, to my mind, is not a reduction in taxation at all. That will increase what is commonly undersood by the people of this country as taxation. The other day the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred to taxation in this country as compared with taxation in Great Britain and other British dominions. The comparison which he gave, with all due respect to his opinion, was not at all applicable to our present condition, because the system of government in those dominions is entirely different, and it is almost an impossibility to arrive at the per capita taxation in this country as compared with that in New Zealand1, for instance. The Minister of Justice shakes his head. He knows that we have a federal government-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member cannot refer to a debate which has been carried on during the same session at a previous time of the session. That is the point exactly. There is no question at all that he can give his reasons.

I was saying that if we do not reduce expenditures in this country, we cannot reduce taxation. I was about to compare the taxation of the country, which is our real competitor, namely the United States, with that of Canada. The Minister of Justice,
I think, stated that our federal taxation was $37 per capita. The taxation in the United States, our real competitor for capital and for industry, is S29 per capita. Until we can approximate the taxation in the United States, we cannot hope to encourage capital to invest in Canada. Capitalists in this country will not invest in industry to-day. They are investing in bonds, tax-free bonds where they can get them. I know of capitalists to-day who are investing in western Canada in investments which they know will not yield an income, relying upon the increased value in the properties they are purchasing in the next ten, twelve or fifteen years, in order to get away from taxation. They (absolutely refuse to invest in any industry to-day on account of, first, taxation and, second, lack of stability in Canada owing to the fiscal policy of this government. For those reasons chiefly, I am opposed to this vote, and I would, therefore, move that resolution No. 139 be reduced by the sum of $1,300,000.

I do not wish to support this resolution by a silent vote, and I would like to make an appeal, futile though it may be, to hon. members on the treasury benches not to force this vote through the House. I think more and more the people of Canada are feeling that if there is possible for us an independent national existence, our
governmental expenses must be cut and cut to the bone. I cannot, for the life of me, see why it should be necessary to make more ample provision for our representation in London than what has proved, perhaps, not sufficient or perfectly adequate, but at least practical, for the last ten or twelve years.
I have no desire to see this government embarrassed, but I have a desire to see them not place themselves flatly in opposition to what I believe to be the views of this country on the question of governmental expenditures. There is only one policy that will satisfy the Canadian people, and that is that anything that we can possibly do without, we should do without in attempting to balance the budget.
I am not familiar witl? the situation in London of these buildings. This may be an excellent building that is proposed. I am not going to deal with the question whether the scheme under ordinary circumstances would be a good scheme or not. The question with me is what expenditure should be incurred of anything but an absolutely essential nature if the country's finances are in the-conditions they are in. I would ask the government to realize that non-essentials must be cut out. I would like to raise my voice in protest against the idea that the prosperity of this country in the future, its importance in the world, is going to be judged by the size or the grandeur of our offices in London or Paris or any other place in the world. The sensible people of this world will think a great deal more of Canada's balance sheet than of Canada's architectural or building possessions in this, that or the other city. I do not wish unduly to take up the time of the committee, but I would implore members on the treasury benches to realize the temperate spirit of the country as regards expenditures and not to endeavour to force this vote through.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no
desire on the part of the government to force anything, but as I intimated a moment ago the lease of the building in which the offices were formerly situated has expired and we are now in temporary quarters. There is not the least doubt that if we go on renting accommodation as we are doing to-day it will cost us much more in the end than if we purchased a building outright. By the purchase of the building we shall save in the way of rents. As pointed out by the minister in charge of the estimates (Mr. King, Kootenay) there will be economies the moment that the different departments are brought within one building. It is perfectly
Supply-Public Works

clear that offices scattered in four different parts of London, none of them in a position at all comparable to this, involve a great deal of waste both in money and time on the part of those engaged in public work in England on behalf of the Dominion and on the part of people who go over to transact business there. The government have gone into this matter very carefully and if we were not convinced that it would make for economy in the long run we would not venture at this time to make the purchase. I think I have given to the House reasons sufficient to show why the chance we have now or a similar chance might not come again. I intimated first of all that a site of this kind is not always available. An hon. member said that the Morley's hotel was a much finer site. I do not know whether he heard me say that that building is to be destroyed; as a matter of fact it is being pulled down to afford a wider space at the entrance to the Strand. The moment that building is removed the value of the property we are acquiring will go up materially. One side of Trafalgar square, as hon. members may know, is occupied by the National Art Gallery, and on the other sides there are the main approaches of London, one down the Strand to the east of London, the other towards Westminster, and yet other approaches to the west of London. Altogether for our purposes there is not a finer site anywhere. An hon. member spoke about the greater part of the traffic being on the other side of the street. Well, that only makes the position of this building all the more advantageous. It is office accommodation that will be required, and it will be very much to the advantage of those who will occupy the building, as well as convenient to persons looking for it, not to be on the crowded side of the street. Moreover, it presents to persons searching for the offices a view of the building much more conspicuous than if the building were located on the congested side
There is another feature of the situation which perhaps is worth noting. My hon. friend who spoke a moment ago (Mr. Mc-Master) is aware of the state in which London exchange has been in the last year, and I can say to the House on fairly good authority that so favourable has the exchange been towards us that having regard to our financial transactions in London we shall save enough out of the difference practically to pay the cost of purchase of the entire building. I have here a communication addressed to me from Mr. Larkin dated February 16, 1924. It is written from the office of the High Commissioner for Canada and reads:

My dear Prime Minister,
Union Club
The enclosed is copy of a letter I have just received from Messrs. Charles Russell and Co., which speaks for itself.
Since the purchase of the building we have saved about $30,000 by not having to pay the money out, as exchange has dropped from 4.70 odd to 4.43, and I think it will come down further. Anyway, I think it would be worth while not sending the money over here until we need it which, as you will see, will be on the 25th of March next. The amount is as set forth in the letter to the Minister of Public Works dated 19th January.
This letter is signed by Mr. Larkin. He points out that since the purchase of the building there has been a saving of some $30,000; that is to say, since the time the option was taken. This is a factor that might be taken into consideration. I see my hon. friend shaking his head. Now, I do not urge it as a reascta, but at least it is a consideration which I think might well appeal to hon. members. In any event the government is committeed to take this building and is prepared to stand or fall by it.
I regret very much that the Prime Minister saw fit to make the statement with which he closed his remarks, that the government would stand or fall by the purchase of this building.

speechtext: No.

Although I have been
following the debate pretty closely, I am yet without certain information. First, we are told that we have an agreement to purchase, then that we have an option. It seems to me that this obscurity should be cleared up for the benefit of the committee. It is either an option or an agreement to purchase. I would ask the minister not to press this vote until 'he has given the committee the floor space of this building with the addition contemplated, and the floor space of the four buildings now occupied as Canadian offices in London. Only then will we be in a position to say whether this proposed building will be sufficiently large to accommodate our offices. Up to now we have nothing to rely on but the hope of the High Commissioner that the building will afford the necessary accommodation. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryekman) seems to be in possession of valuable information as to the location of the building in question, much more possibly than that possessed by many hon. members who have already spoken and who have advised as to the necessity of hurrying forward the purchase. Before any hon. member can give an in-

telligent vote upon this enormous expenditure of $1,300,000-at a time when we are all preaching, and wish to practise, economy-we must have the information called for this evening.

It seem3 to me that we are in danger of overlooking what is actually a very grave departure from proper practice in connection with this transaction. Does anybody know the date of the order in council under which the contract was made? Does anybody know under what pretended authority the country was committed to a contract involving the expenditure of this large sum of money without the slightest expression of opinion from parliament? I would ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), what is the legal justification for this alleged contract? Can he tell me? He cannot, simply because there is not any. And this from the party that was going to be so very constitutional, the party which was going to do nothing of which parliament did not first approve-this party pledged the honour of the country and themselves without the slightest parliamentary authority. And it is not as if this were the only case of its kind.. We were given an illustration of it last session when we had the case of the Scribe hotel; and here we have another purchase apparently without the slightest authority. If there is any, can we get it? Is the cabinet absolutely dumb?
I would like to refer them to their own protestations, to what they themselves said hundreds of times when they were on this side. I would refer them to some of the utterances of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister about autocracy, about the usurpation of power, the responsibilities of government, the rights of the people, control by parliament, and the iniquities of orders in council. Yet here we have these very same gentlemen apparently ready to spend over a million dollars absolutely without authority. I am going to ask again-perhaps I can get an answer this time

what is the date of the order in council authorizing this agreement?

The matter was brought forward purposely at that time in order that the High Commissioner might receive instructions whether he should proceed with the negotiations which, as I mentioned to the House at the time, were in progress. Having brought the matter up in the House and having had it discussed here, the government instructed the High Commissioner to proceed with the negotiations. As I think I mentioned on that occasion, it was not advisable to have undue publicity in connection with the effort to obtain particular buildings; that if they were to be purchased at a satisfactory price it would not be wise to^ advertise the circumstances too freely to intending vendors. The whole matter was discussed in the House last session, and the government certainly took it from the discussion that the members of the House were in favour of the purchase of a building in London; indeed, the expressions of opinion given were practically all to that effect. The High Commissioner was instructed to go ahead with the negotiations. He kept the government fully informed, step by step, of what he was doing. The government authorized him to enter into an agreement which would give us the right to obtain this property. We have not yet put through an order in council acquiring the property, but one will be passed as soon as this amount is voted.

Surely my right hon. friend is not serious when he says he has no authority for the making of this contract. There was talk about purchasing something- it might have been about the purchase of anything. There was no vote, there was nothing which anyone coming into this House for the first time in his life could refer to as an authority for anything. So we now learn that Mr. Larkin was instructed to sign the contract; it is a contract which Mr. Larkin has entered into on the authority of instructions of the government. How did the instructions get to Mr. Larkin? Which department looks after that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Department of Public Works.

I do not know that there has ever been a precedent for this situation in the history of this parliament. It is apparent from the confessions of the government, although some of the confessions are wholly contradictory to others previously made, that

Supply-Public "Works

they have actually a contract signed, an absolutely binding contract under which this country undertakes to pay 11,300,000 in England. I do not think a member of the government dares to get up and dispute that. That is the position we find ourselves in tonight-not even a contract in which there is a clause making it subject to the vote of parliament and thereby relieving us of damages in the event of the vote not being taken. And the Prime Minister says, "We have authority to do it, because I mentioned it a year ago; because I said we were thinking of buying a building somewhere in London." This is the responsible government for which the battle was fought in 1921. Let us all be careful; let us listen to-every word that falls from the lips of the Prime Minister and from every member of the government; for if they venture to express the hope that some day we will own something we may expect the next year to find ourselves bound hand and foot and the money practically sent over. Really I cannot conceive of a member of a government making a plea of that kind before an intelligent committee. Talk about responsible government! Certainly a government must make contracts. Sometimes it is bound to do so in emergencies; sometimes it even has to call in the aid of Governor General's warrants. But in a case of that kind it makes its contract subject to the will of parliament. It does not come to parliament and say, we are tied hand and foot and we have either got to stand or fall-and "O, what a fall was there, my countrymen!" if this government actually fell. The government has no sense of its responsibilities when it ties the hands of this parliament, making us mere automatons, putting us in a position where we have no say at all, binding us to an investment overseas in respect of which not a single member of parliament outside the government had the faintest knowledge and with regard to which we have mighty little knowledge even yet. That is the position the committee finds itself in now, landed there by a government elected to restore -mark the word-to restore responsible government in Canada, to gather the shattered remnants-
We have not yet spent five million dollars on graving docks to elect a minister of the Crown.
No, I do not think you have spent $5,000,000 on graving docks, but you are spending it as fast as you can on that graving dock, and your minister says you should have spent it sooner.
That dock only elected a member of the government which was in office for but a few months.

Yes, and the Minister
of Public Works censured us a year ago because we had not gone ahead with it sooner, declared that we had thereby lost a lot of business for Canada, declared that was the only fault he could find with it. However, we had better not get slid off into a graving dock. Whatever we did we had the authority of parliament for, and I would like to see the authority of parliament produced for this.	.. ,

made. That is the hon. member's idea of responsible	government-have	ourselves
bound with chains and then told, you have to do it, the honour of the country is bound, and all you are here for is to do it; and the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) is slave enough to come right Up to the mark and do it.

The hon. gentleman and

Never; not at all. The
hon. member's memory is very weak. There was nothing done there except it was expressly stated to be subject to the vote of parliament.

But the contract had been
entered into.
That clause left parliament free. Is parliament free to-night?
Undoubtedly.

Free? When the minister tells us there is an absolutely binding contract and that the country will have to pay damages if the money is not voted, and we are liable to specific performance? That is the position we are in to-night.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his law for that?
I get it principally from the fountains of common sense.

The hon. member thinks
law and common sense are one and the same thing, and he is a lawyer.

My sense of law is common sense; I am afraid the hon. member's sometimes is not. The position is this:If we are bound and there is no relieving clause making it subject to the vote of parliament, why are we not liable to specific performance?
Whom will they sue?

Sue us unless we refuse
a fiat, as the Minister of Justice did last session in the Marshall case. That is the only way we could get out of it, and it is not a very honourable way. Now we know the position we are in, and we know who have placed us in this position.

We have to-night
the remarkable spectacle of the Prime Minister making the direct statement that this country is committed to the purchase of this property, and immediately afterwards the 44 i
Minister of Public Works, under whose department this matter comes, informing the House that the country is not committed, that it has an option and the option is going to expire in about three minutes. Now we are given to understand that the functions of this parliament are simply to ratify what the government does. This
12 midnight is their sense of responsible government which we have heard so very much about. We all remember how the Prime Minister and those associated with him toured this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific a short time ago denouncing the autocracy of hon. members who now occupy this side of the House. If ever there was a clear case of autocracy and of contempt for parliament it is exhibited in the action of the government in this matter. I am surprised that certain members of the government can sit in their seats and listen to the directly contradictory statements that have been made by their colleagues and expect parliament to vote this $1,300,000 through without any further discussion.
We have heard arguments advanced why this vote should be passed. The Prime Minister himself admits that the property is not a desirable one unless the property adjoining it can be secured at some time in the future, and he has no assurance that it can be secured. He has not been able to show the House that it can be secured. We have heard the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) telling the House that it is going to be a good investment. You would think that this government were annoyed with all the money they have on their hands for investment, and that they had no idea what to do with it. We have been told that it is going to be a great advertisement for Canada, that there are many people over in the Old Land who have not heard of Canada, but who when they see this building in the middle of London will be coming out here by the thousands. Immigration is going to be furthered, we are told, by this purchase. I notice that the estimates for Immigration and Colonization this year are $2,000,000 more than the estimates for the same purpose in 19211922. We are dealing in millions to-day as we used to deal with thousands formerly. Have the government lost all sense of the position of this country at the present time? Have they forgotten about the enormous deficits which have daily to be met? I quite agree with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) that it is our duty to pare down to the bone everything that can possibly be pared. We must cut expenses as fine as we possibly can.

In view of what happened with regard to the item for $600,000 which was put through the House a few hours ago, I should not be at all surprised if the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), after a night's rest, would vote a different way from what he has intimated tonight. I challenge the hon. member's statement that I voted differently from what I said I would do.
I understood the hon. member to say that if he was going to vote on this he was going to vote against it.
I want your ruling, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member said that I voted differently from what I said I would do on the $600,000 item. I never made the statement that I would vote against that item.

I may be a little in error in that. I think the hon. gentleman intimated that he would support a vote to reduce the item by $100,000, as I think Hansard will show; but he could not support a motion to reduce it by $75,000 or $50,000.
I made the statement that the government might reduce it by $100,000, but I never made the statement that I would not vote for the $600,000 item.

We have extracted, practically with a corkscrew, so much information from the government during the last hour that if the matter stands over for another day we may be able to get some more information regarding it. If this option was to expire to-night it shows why the government are so anxious to have this vote pass, the first item of the estimates they introduced into the House. Why were the government not frank? Why did they not inform us that an option had been secured on this property, and that it would expire at a certain time? But we have the assurance of the Prime Minister that the government are committed to this enterprise absolutely, and all that parliament is called upon to do is to vote the money. Is that treating parliament as it should be treated? Is the function of parliament merely to ratify what the government bring forward, even though the House is in session and has a right to be informed of all that has transpired? And the Minister of Public Works informs us that the option expires on the 25th March. Who are we to believe, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Public Works? One or the other is not correct in his statements. Consequently I say we are entitled to have the contract in 
this matter placed before us so that we may ascertain the facts. If we cannot take the word of members of the government in regard to a subject of this kind, we ought to have in our possession the document under which the country is committed to the expenditure before we pass this vote.

Coming back to a question we discussed earlier in the evening, namely the facilities for gathering round this building the various provincial offices, I should like to ask what is the size of the adjoining lot, the lot occupied, I think, by the building of the College of Physicians. I have been in that building and my recollection of it is that the lot is not a large one. I should like to have information on that point if the minister is in a position to give it.
I have not the dimensions of the adjoining lot. Some hon. members who have seen the building may be able to give that information.

I did not hear the
minister, will he please repeat his statement?
I say I have not the extent of the adjoining lot, that information is not here.

Well, that is a very
important omission. If it is a small lot it will not be sufiiciently large to permit the grouping of the various provincial offices of the Dominion and that, I believe, would cause profound disappointment in the country. I should like to have a clear understanding of the question as it stands. Has this property been bought or is it under option?
There is an agreement to purchase.
If the sale is not completed by March 25, what will happen then? Will the sale be off or are we still liable?

We have agreed
to buy.

There are two or three matters I should like to submit. In the first place I can hardly think the minister, or the government, will want to put this item through without supplying some needed information. I think it will be admitted by everybody that we have a somewhat unusual situation in connection with this property. I am going to assume now that what we have is an agreement; if I am wrong I may be corrected. I think we ought to know the date of it, and who signed it. I presume the minister has a copy of the agreement before him, and I certainly should like to see it. I should

also like to see who signed the document on behalf of Canada. Further I should like to find out who sent the authority to London, if it was sent there, for the completion of this agreement. I presume, in the first instance that some person on behalf of the department, or the government, had an investigation made regarding this building, and the terms upon which it could be purchased. I also presume that information was sent over and was duly considered. I understand there was no order in council passed. Was there even a letter signed by the minister, or by any responsible person on behalf of the government, authorizing the closing of this contract? Now, who signed it pursuant to that letter, and under what authority? I think before we are asked to pass an item involving 11,300,000 we are entitled to this information. If it cannot be given now-the minister I see nods his head so I will be pleased to sit down in order to get the information. If there is no objection I should like very much if the minister would be good enough to let a copy of the agreement, or the agreement itself, be passed over here for us to look at.

There was an agreement signed on the 26th June, 1923, between Charles Drummond, 49 Charing Cross, and General Sir William Henry Mackinnon, Sir Bertram Blakiston Cubitt, and Sir Lawrence Edward Halsey, on behalf of the trustees of the Union Club, and the Hon. Peter Charles Larkin, High Commissioner, on behalf of Canada.

What was the
date?
The date was 26th June, 1923.

I appreciate that information which answers my question as far as it goes. But the minister has not given me any in-foAnation regarding the nature of the authority sent to Mr. Larkin to sign the agreement on behalf of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If hon. gentlemen opposite really wished to get the true position of the matter they would have ascertained from my remarks a moment ago that in a transaction of this kind it is necessary for the government to trust to some agent and to have the negotiations carried on as quietly as possible. If you are negotiating a purchase for the government it does not do to proclaim the matter from the house tops, it is necessary to trust your agent or your representative in matters of the kind. I mentioned that last session the government
discussed in the House the intended purchase of a building in London. The building we were trying to acquire at the time, or that we thought of acquiring, was Cox's Bank, the price, however, was much higher than we expected. It would have been a building that would have accommodated the different provinces as well as the federal government. We found that a commission was being claimed by a certain party in London on the purchase of that building, and as soon as the High Commissioner learned that a commission was to be made by someone he immediately ended the negotiations without further discussion. He then continued to see what might be possible with respect to the Union Club; he had been negotiating with respect to different buildings. In case the Cox building should not be acquired he had been inquiring also about the Union Club building, He did not know whether we could get the Union Club building. In connection with the acquisition of the Union Club building, it was necessary to have arrangements made with the club itself involving the taking of a vote on the part of the members whether they would dispose of the Club building. Matters of that kind rendered necessary the giving of some assurance on the part of the government that the building would be acquired subsequently, and the government authorized Mr. Larkin to proceed with the negotiations, to keep us informed as to the price at which the building could be obtained, and he would receive further advice as the government got additional particulars. At each step of the negotiations, Mr. Larkin kept the government informed by cable and he received his replies by cable. He made the agreement for the purchase. He is the High Commissioner for Canada. If any government official is entitled to the confidence of the government and the country, it is surely the High Commissioner of this country in England. If there is one business man above another who has had experience in large transactions of the kind and who knows values in the matter of the purchase of a building, that person is the Hon. Mr. Larkin. The government had entire confidence in his judgment, business ability and acumen in this matter, and we therefore entrusted him to make what was necessary in the way of agreements to secure the purchase of the building.

I have one observation to make on the Prime Minister's remarks. The government knowing that Mr. Larkin was going to purchase this building, knowing that he had been authorized to purchase and

knowing that he had actually signed a contract to purchase it, before the House prorogued last session, it seems a remarkable thing to me that the Prime Minister did not take the House into his confidence and tell us that a contract had been entered into.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I answer my hon, friend right there? I think I said a moment ago that, in a transaction of this kind', several stages were necessary. Knowing the Prime Minister's declared policy, in regard to forcing votes or measures through this House without due consideration, I am sure he will be the last one to attempt to force this vote through to-night. Mr. Larkin bound Canada to a contract for the purchase of this building, and that in that contract is contained a clause that it was subject to the ratification of members of the Union Club, but not subject to the ratification of parliament?

That was the Union Club building that I was referring to. I am reading from Hansard of June 29, 1923:
Mr. Baxter: Sir Henry Thornton may possibly have bought a castle or two in London, and perhaps the thing may come in that way.
Mr. Ross (Kingston): May I ask whether the question will be considered of assembling all the Canadian offices in London? It seems too bad that the Ontario office should be in the Strand, the British Columbia offices in Pall Mall, and the High Commissioner's office in Victoria street. It struck me as being too bad that a similar situation could not be created for Canada.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I am glad my hon. friend asked that question because he has reminded me of the fact that last year we tried to acquire the British Columbia building. The federal government would have been prepared to take that building over had the British Columbia government been willing to part with it, but they have found that in that large building, which is so favourably located, they have an excellent investment; as a matter of fact I think they are making money on it. The present situation is that Canada has a much inferior building to that maintained in London by one of its provinces. The federal government rents part of the British Columbia building for offices connected with immigration work. The government has felt that Canada has been handicapped as compared with the other dominions in having its offices scattered about in various buildings throughout London-not only the offices of the different provinces, but the different federal offices that were created during the war. The office which has to do with the soldiers' overseas work is in one part of the city. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has offices for his agents in another part of the city. The immigration offices are in still another part and the High Commissioner's offices are elsewhere. We felt that it was desirable to acquire a building in which all these offices could be brought together and which would be large enough also to accommodate the representatives of the different provinces, but that kind of a building in London is not easily acquired, and rather than make a purchase which would not meet with the general approval of the country we have proceeded slowly in the matter. But the object is to do the very thing my hon. friend has 'said-to acquire a building that will serve all these purposes in a way that will reflect credit on the country.
That was three days after the contract was signed?

Mr. Mackenzie King: I cannot say that an option has not been secured. I think the High Commissioner has arranged that at any rate before a certain building is disposed of he will be given the refusal of it. More than that I cannot say.
More than that I could not say then, because I had not the knowledge. These matters were under negotiation in the way I have indicated. My point is that the matter was discussed in a frank, open manner, and in view of the fact that the government having tried the year before to purchase the British Columbia building, but without success, and then having endeavoured to secure the Cox building, it was the duty of hon. gentlemen at that time, if they considered that we were not proceeding in the right way, to have said so.

Let me read what the
Prime Minister said. I asked the following question:

friend read further down:

Apparently the Prime
Minister has two or three ways of answering a question, but it does not matter a fig what particular words he uses.
Oh, oh.

I do not see that there is much reason for the hilarity of hon. gentlemen opposite-evidently a million dollars does not matter much to them. The question

was asked whether an option had been secured, and it does not matter whether the Prime Minister answered yes or no, or whether he said, "I do not know," or " I am not aware."
