I am.
We are not discussing a post mortem.

I know that this country had to pay damages in that case; a government which my hon. friend supported paid damages just because there was no relief. But is it not remarkable that we cannot have a look at the contract? The honour of Canada is bound in this matter and the government has virtually admitted over and over again that the excuse is that there was some talk by the Prime Minister last session about the wisdom of getting a building. That is his authority to go ahead. Hon. gentlemen opposite are very much interested in the contract. One after another reads it, but hon. members on this side of the House are not allowed to see it. Why can it not go on Hansard to-night? Surely the people's representatives have a right to see just what the contract is.
If the contract is to be read at all let it be read audibly.

It is to be
observed, Mr. Chairman, the fidelity with
Supply-Public Works

which the trustees of the Union Club discharged their trust, it is to be observed that they took very good care that their shareholders were to have the opportunity of saying whether they liked the contract or not, and this is all the more noticeable when we observe the absolute failure on the part of our representatives to incorporate a similar provision for securing the approval of the parliament of Canada. The case is worse than where there has been an ordinary overriding of parliament, because not even ignorance can be pleaded here. You have gentlemen on the one side who are looking after the people whom they represent and are making sure that their rights are protected, while no such degree of consideration is given in connection with Canada. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier said a good deal about the country not being bound. In one sense he is quite right, but in the other sense is there anything at all in what he says? There is an absolutely hard and fast, carefully drawn agreement which entirely binds the Canadian High Commissioner. Why the country is without any plea, the government is without any plea as against him. They told him to do it, so that the commissioner certainly is bound, and the government is in honour bound to make good any loss that he might suffer in connection with a transaction which he put through under their instructions. So we know what this contract is; it is exactly what was suggested before. I wonder if the Prime Minister thinks he should force a vote on this question now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If I felt for one moment that hon. members had not had ample opportunity to discuss the matter I should certainly say that such further time should be granted as might be necessary for the purpose. I am very sincere when I say that the government is anxious to get on with the business of the country. We have spent a good deal of time over one or two items and we would like to get this estimate through to-night. I am not going to try to force it through, but I do submit that in the interests of the country, in the interests of economy, of which my hon. friends opposite have been speaking so much, it is desirable that the government should get the estimate through. The government will take the full responsibility for its action in this matter. This building could not have been acquired in any other way and the government, having all the circumstances before it, took the course which it believed to be in the public interest. My hon. friend says that the Union Club protected

itself, and asks why some clause was not put in the agreement under which the parliament. of Canada at such and such a time should exercise certain rights. If that clause had been put in, the agreement never could have been signed. There was just one chance of the government being able to secure that property, and it was a question of the government giving the High Commissioner the latitude which was necessary to enable him to make the purchase. We believed that the purchase would commend itself to the country, and knowing all the circumstances we felt that we were taking the right course in authorizing the High Commissioner to make the agreement that was entered into. If that agreement is not honoured certainly the country is not honouring its obligation. The government feels bound to stand by its obligation. As I say, we cannot be a government if we have no authority. If I had not discussed the matter fully last session and intimated what we were contemplating at that time, I would bow in a moment to what has been said about trying in any way to ignore parliament. But I submit that we have gone very fully into the matter; we have taken parliament into our confidence and have made a bargain which I believe the people of Canada will regard more and more as the years go by as one of the best investments which could have been made for the country.

My right hon.
friend appeals to me on the ground of economy. If I answered him from the same point of view I would have to tell him frankly that the cheapest way out of this difficulty is to pay your damage and refuse the vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We need the building; we have no premises. My hon. friend forgets that the lease of the building we were in had expired, and that we had to rent temporary quarters in the meantime. These are all factors that bear on the situation.
Could the lease not have been renewed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It could have been renewed for another seven or eight years, but it was thought unwise in the interests of Canada to renew a lease on Victoria street for that further period.
Could it not have been renewed for five years?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No.

Supply-Public Works

I think the Prime
Minister intimated earlier in the discussion that it could.

There is one matter on
which I would like some information, and it is information upon which my vote in the matter will depend. Could this property have been secured on an option.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: From what Mr. Larkin has told us I do not think the property could have been secured in any other way. I think he had to be in a position to assure the Union Club that the' government would take the property if the membership of the club gave the executive permission to sell. That was the only way he could get it. The property being what and where it is, situated, as has been intimated to-night, on Trafalgar Square, the leasehold being from the Crowntaking all these facts into consideration, and having in mind that we were getting a site not for a day but for years and possibly centuries to come, the government felt justified in authorizing Mr. Larkin to proceed.

Was a copy of the
contract-I mean a duplicate-handed over to the trustees of the Union Club at the time of execution?
I suppose so.

The Prime Minister seeks to persuade us that the government simply had to proceed as it did; that otherwise a great chance might be lost forever; that we had to do it, though we had not the vote of parliament, though we had not the slightest semblance of authority. Well, it does seem to me that the correspondence that led up to what finally authorized the execution of an agreement on that basis should be brought down. I must admit for my part that it does not matter what the correspondence is, no government had the right to tie this country to an expenditure of that sort, placing the High Commissioner in a position where he had to put up every cent, having no authority from parliament to proceed. The government knew that the lease was expiring; if they felt it was a fearful thing to stay on in this place why did they not come last session and ask for a vote of parliament? That is the procedure that is followed every session. We may plan to erect a public building here or there, we do not know just on what site; a vote of parliament is asked for, and on that vote the government proceeds. In this case nothing is asked for at all; the government, in effect, affixes the seal of this Dominion to a contract involving the expenditure of a vast sum of
money, and parliament is in the position of helplessly having to support it-except as regards those who want to protest against that method of carrying on the public business.
I think we ought at least to have the correspondence, and further I think that every hon. member owes it to the country to record himself in this matter. We should not come to a decision to-night but rather at a time when hon. members can be present and record themselves yea or nay.
What was the date of the contract?
The twenty-sixth of June.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The House will remember that a year ago last November or December the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was in England; he had been at the conference in Geneva and was subsequently in London. While in London he took this matter up with the High Commissioner. The Minister of Finance was himself very strongly in favour of the purchase of the Grand Hotel, which is on the other side of Trafalgar Square, and that was one of the buildings which the government thought of acquiring. We found, however, that to purchase the Grand Hotel would mean an expenditure away out of consideration, and that project was not pursued any further The Minister of Finance, I think, is as careful of the honour of the country, of the responsibility of the Ministry to parliament, as any hon. member of this House has ever been or ever will be, and the Minister of Finance was present in the cabinet when all these transactions were discussed, was a party to the communications that were sent to Mr. Larkin, and I think he would have been the first had he thought it was in the public interest to disclose the fact that Canada was seeking to make this purchase, to have placed a sum in the estimates at the time .My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) asks why we did not put it in the estimates. He knows why we did not. We were trying to make the best bargain possible for this country, and if a cable despatch had gone from Canada to England that the Canadian government was appropriating $1,500,000 for the purchase of a building in London that would have ended in five minutes all the negotiations Mr. Larkin was making with any hope of getting a contract consummated at a reasonable figure. I ask hon. members as business men to concede to the government the right to proceed in these matters with the same degree of caution and in the same manner as they would
Supply-Public Works

proceed in their own private business transactions when carried on in a large way. If they are prepared to do that, I think they will agree that the government in this matter have had the public interests to the fore at every stage of the transaction.
As to the matter of bringing down correspondence there is no reason why all the correspondence should not be brought down, but unless hon. gentlemen are merely seeking to obstruct this vote there is no reason why it should not go through to-night. If there is anything in the correspondence or in the transaction for which the government should be condemned hon. members will have the rest of the session to bring in a resolution in regard to that, but I do submit that if we are to save the money of this country by getting through with the business of parliament, and we have spent a good part of the day on this one item already, it would be quite justifiable to have this vote go through to-night rather than have the<matter held up further.

May I point out to the Prime Minister that any delay there has been was the result of the government not being frank with us. Let me give to him exactly what we were told when this discussion opened on Thursday. After reciting a lot of matter that was not germane to this immediate point the minister went on to say:
Investigations were carried on in regard to that building but the price was considered higher than we were prepared to pay. Later on the High Commissioner suggested that the Union Club building could be secured, and this estimate is for the purpose of purchasing that building.
A very innocent remark, but why did not the minister produce the contract and tell us exactly what the Prime Minister has told us in the last half hour or so. If he had done so, I venture to say there would have been far less discussion, whatever our views may have been. It has not been by obstruction but only by persistent cross-examination that we have been able to get the information that should have been produced by the government without a question being asked as soon as the vote was called. This information and this contract should have been before parliament at that time and the Prime Minister must bear me out in this,
' that it is only by the most persistent crossexamination that we have been able to obtain only the most ordinary information that is given upon all items that come up for discussion. That is what we complain of, and that is what our criticism of the government is, as much as the other phase of the question, the inadvisability of the purchase as well as

the fact that the purchase does not represent what the government hopes it will accomplish. That I persist in reiterating. If it did, there might be some justification for the government's persistence, but it will not accomplish it, and personally I think the government deserves censure for the manner in which this whole vote has been handled on Thursday and to-day. There has been nothing but a resistance against getting the most ordinary information.

I wish to say that my vote in opposition to this is not with the intention of obstruction. I 1 a.m. took the position last year, and I think my question last year will show it, that I considered the proposition was to enter into the purchase of a building which would represent all Canada and combine all the provincial offices. That was distinctly stated. Now we are not told to-night that any effort has ever been made to get together all the provinces except the province of British Columbia. I wish to point out further that if this building is purchased it forever prevents us realizing the vision we had of all getting together, because there is not accommodation there for the provincial offices, and it will simply mean that the Dominion government will be in one office and the provincial offices will be spread all over London. If we purchase this building we are preventing the realization of that vision we had, and which we all want to see realized. Amendment negatived. Yeas, 31; Nays, 56.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the main motion.

The item includes the
three figures?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The first two items have passed, and the question is now on the last item for the Canadian building in London.

I wish to have a vote
on that.

I understood the Prime
Minister to say that he would lay the correspondence on the Table to-morrow if a vote was taken to-night. Is it understood that that correspondence will be laid on the table tomorrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Item carried on division. Yeas, 57, Nays, 32. Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 1.01 a.m. (Wednesday).
